case: A 57-year-old female without any medical history was admitted for evaluation of a left ventricular tumor that was discovered incidentally. The patient was asymptomatic and had no relevant past medical history. Physical examination findings were not specifically described in the case report.

Cardiac fibroma.description: A benign fibrous tumor usually located within ventricular muscle. It is more common in children but can be discovered incidentally in adults.

Left ventricular myxoma.description: A benign primary cardiac tumor that usually arises in an atrium but occasionally develops in the left ventricle. Imaging is needed to characterize its attachment and mobility.

Cardiac lipoma.description: A benign tumor composed of mature fat that can develop within the myocardium or cardiac chambers and often causes no symptoms.

Papillary fibroelastoma.description: A benign cardiac tumor typically attached to a valve, although it can arise from the ventricular endocardium. It may be incidental or cause embolic complications.

Left ventricular thrombus.description: A blood clot within the left ventricle that can mimic a tumor on imaging. It usually occurs with impaired ventricular contraction, myocardial infarction, or an apical aneurysm.

case: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.

Left lower lobe pneumonia.description: Infection of the lower left lung can irritate the adjacent diaphragm and cause upper abdominal pain in children, sometimes without obvious chest examination findings or leukocytosis.

Acute pleuritis.description: Inflammation of the lining around the lungs, often associated with a respiratory infection, can cause sharp pain with breathing and referred upper abdominal pain.

Splenic abscess.description: A localized infection within the spleen can cause fever and left upper quadrant pain, including pain with breathing from diaphragmatic irritation. It is uncommon in otherwise healthy children.

Splenic infarction.description: Interruption of blood flow to part of the spleen causes tissue injury and left upper quadrant pain. It is rare in a healthy child without a hematologic, vascular, or embolic risk factor.

Acute pericarditis.description: Inflammation of the sac surrounding the heart typically causes pleuritic pain that worsens when lying flat. Children occasionally present with upper abdominal rather than chest pain.

case: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

Splenic abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection of the spleen that may cause fever and diaphragmatic irritation; abdominal imaging is needed to assess this possibility.

Melioidosis.description: Infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, acquired particularly in tropical northern Australia and Southeast Asia. It can cause pneumonia, systemic infection, or visceral abscesses and occasionally presents after a prolonged latent interval.

Legionella pneumonia.description: A bacterial pneumonia associated with environmental water exposure that can produce prominent systemic and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of a pulmonary artery by a clot, potentially associated with prolonged travel. It can cause pleuritic pain and breathlessness despite a normal chest radiograph.

Acute Q fever.description: Coxiella burnetii infection, usually acquired through inhalation of contaminated animal-associated aerosols. It occurs in Australia and may cause a febrile illness, pneumonia, or hepatitis.

Nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis.normalized_text: Nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis with possible invasive infection
Nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis.description: A foodborne bacterial infection causing diarrhea and fever; invasive disease can occasionally produce bloodstream infection or focal abscesses.

case: A 60-year-old white Caucasian woman presented with a 4-year history of worsening gait and sensory disturbance accompanied by urinary urgency and nocturia. She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

Primary progressive multiple sclerosis.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause steadily progressive spinal cord dysfunction and optic nerve injury. MRI findings and exclusion of alternative causes are needed for diagnosis.

OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.normalized_text: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome
OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus.description: An inherited mitochondrial disorder causing progressive optic neuropathy, sometimes accompanied by spasticity, neuropathy, ataxia or other neurological manifestations.

SPG7-related complicated hereditary spas.description: A genetic neurodegenerative disorder that can produce adult-onset progressive spastic paraplegia with optic neuropathy, sensory abnormalities and sometimes cerebellar ataxia.

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with a.normalized_text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with an MS-like syndrome (Harding disease)
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with a.description: A mitochondrial optic neuropathy occurring with an inflammatory demyelinating syndrome resembling multiple sclerosis, particularly in women.

Aquaporin-4-seronegative neuromyelitis o.description: An inflammatory disorder primarily affecting the optic nerves and spinal cord. Negative aquaporin-4 antibodies do not completely exclude it, but seronegative cases require stringent clinical and MRI criteria.

case: A 14-year-old female patient presented with generalized pruritus accompanied by scleral icterus and petechiae/ecchymoses on the extremities for over 2 months. She had no fever, abdominal pain, or distension. Past medical history included amenorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and acne. She had been taking Chinese herbal medicines (specific components unknown) for approximately 9 months. Physical examination revealed clear consciousness, facial acne and pigmentation, mild scleral and mucocutaneous jaundice, soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound tenderness, and no lower extremity edema.

Herbal medicine–induced liver injury wit.normalized_text: Herbal medicine–induced liver injury with cholestasis
Herbal medicine–induced liver injury wit.description: Liver injury caused by herbal ingredients, contaminants, or adulterants. The prolonged herbal medicine exposure makes this a leading consideration, although laboratory testing and exclusion of other causes are necessary.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: Immune-mediated liver inflammation that can occur in adolescent girls and cause jaundice, impaired liver function, and chronic endocrine disturbances.

Wilson disease with hepatic involvement.description: An inherited disorder of copper metabolism that can produce liver disease during childhood or adolescence, sometimes before neurological symptoms develop.

Autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis.description: An autoimmune liver disorder seen in children and adolescents that combines bile duct inflammation and scarring with features of autoimmune hepatitis.

Viral hepatitis with a prolonged cholest.normalized_text: Viral hepatitis with a prolonged cholestatic course
Viral hepatitis with a prolonged cholest.description: Viral liver inflammation, including hepatitis A or E, can occasionally cause prolonged jaundice and itching. Viral testing is needed to distinguish this from medication-related and autoimmune injury.

case: A 66-year-old man presented with 2 days of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. His history included hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; he had started azathioprine 75 mg 10 days earlier. On examination, he was febrile (38°C) with bilateral tender knees and a patellar tap. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, elevated CRP and ESR, mildly elevated rheumatoid factor, and negative anti-CCP, dsDNA, ENA, and ASO tests. Renal function and urinalysis were normal, chest radiograph was normal, and synovial fluid was noninflammatory with no bacteria or crystals.

Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome.description: A drug-triggered acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by painful inflammatory skin lesions, fever, and neutrophilia. The timing after azathioprine initiation strongly supports this possibility; skin biopsy is needed for confirmation.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome.description: An idiosyncratic systemic reaction usually occurring within the first few weeks of azathioprine treatment, causing fever, rash, malaise, and musculoskeletal symptoms. It may overlap with drug-induced Sweet syndrome.

Drug-induced serum sickness-like reactio.description: A medication-associated inflammatory reaction featuring fever, rash, and joint pain, generally developing one to three weeks after exposure. Unlike classic serum sickness, renal involvement is usually absent.

Drug-induced cutaneous small-vessel vasc.description: Inflammation of dermal small vessels triggered by a medication, typically producing palpable purpura and sometimes fever and arthralgias. Skin biopsy establishes the diagnosis.

Acute viral arthritis with exanthem.description: A systemic viral infection, such as parvovirus B19 infection, can cause an acute rash, fever, fatigue, and polyarticular joint pain.

case: A 60-year-old woman presented after sustaining direct trauma to the anterior neck from a fall. She developed progressively worsening hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and pain with neck movement. Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.

Traumatic retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding into the space behind the pharynx after neck trauma, causing progressive compression of the swallowing passage and potentially life-threatening airway obstruction.

Blunt laryngeal injury with possible lar.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal injury with possible laryngeal cartilage fracture
Blunt laryngeal injury with possible lar.description: Traumatic injury to the laryngeal framework and surrounding tissues, potentially producing hematoma, edema, vocal dysfunction, and airway compromise.

Traumatic thyroid hemorrhage.description: Bleeding within or around the thyroid gland following anterior neck trauma, which can compress the trachea, esophagus, or laryngeal nerves.

Traumatic hypopharyngeal perforation.description: A tear in the hypopharyngeal wall after blunt trauma, potentially allowing air and swallowed material to enter deep neck tissues and cause dangerous swelling or infection.

Traumatic cervical vascular injury with.normalized_text: Traumatic cervical vascular injury with expanding neck hematoma
Traumatic cervical vascular injury with.description: Injury to a cervical artery or vein causing an enlarging hematoma that may compress the pharynx and airway.

case: 37-year-old man with 3 months of recurrent episodes of weakness, irritability, poor concentration, craving for sweets, fogginess, cold clammy sensation, and fatigue, often after several hours առանց food, especially at night or early morning. His wife noted abnormal behavior and prolonged memory loss. He gained 30 lb during this period from drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. He had similar symptoms several days before at another hospital. Past history was unremarkable except umbilical hernia repair and back surgery 10 years earlier; no medication use, no smoking, social alcohol use, no illicit drugs. Family history was positive for diabetes. On examination he was confused, cold, and clammy; other physical findings were unremarkable. CBC, electrolytes, renal and liver tests were normal; HbA1c was 5%. Short synacthen test ruled out adrenal insufficiency. Calcium and parathyroid hormone were normal; prolactin was mildly elevated, with normal FSH, LH, and TSH. MRCP showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular slightly exophytic lesion arising anteriorly between the head and neck of the pancreas.

Pancreatic insulinoma.description: An insulin-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor causing recurrent hypoglycemia, typically during fasting. This is the leading diagnosis given the symptom pattern and hypervascular pancreatic lesion; confirmation requires glucose, insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin measurements during an episode.

Non-insulinoma pancreatogenous hypoglyce.description: A rare disorder of pancreatic beta-cell hyperfunction, sometimes associated with nesidioblastosis, that causes endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia without a discrete insulinoma.

Insulin autoimmune syndrome.description: Insulin-binding autoantibodies cause fluctuating insulin availability and spontaneous hypoglycemia, often after meals but occasionally during fasting.

Sulfonylurea- or meglitinide-induced hyp.description: Exposure to insulin-secretagogue medications can cause prolonged or recurrent endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and mimic insulinoma; a drug screen during hypoglycemia helps distinguish them.

Exogenous insulin-induced hypoglycemia.description: Injected insulin can cause recurrent hypoglycemia, whether through accidental or undisclosed exposure. High insulin with suppressed C-peptide during documented hypoglycemia supports this diagnosis.

case: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: Excessive mobility of the lower costal cartilages, usually involving ribs 8–10, can irritate intercostal nerves and cause episodic lower chest wall pain.

Abdominal wall or intercostal muscle str.normalized_text: Abdominal wall or intercostal muscle strain
Abdominal wall or intercostal muscle str.description: Overuse or minor injury of the abdominal or intercostal muscles and their rib attachments can cause localized pain during muscle contraction.

Rib stress fracture.description: Repetitive loading can cause a small rib fracture without a single traumatic injury, particularly after an increase in training intensity.

Costochondritis.description: Painful irritation of the rib-to-cartilage or cartilage-to-sternum junctions, sometimes associated with repetitive upper-body exercise.

Intercostal neuralgia.description: Irritation or compression of an intercostal nerve can cause sharp, shooting, or burning pain along the chest wall.

case: A 31-year-old woman underwent barium enema examination as part of a medical checkup. She had been healthy without specific complaints and had no significant past medical or family history. The patient was 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg, appeared well, and the physical examination showed no abnormalities. Complete blood cell count and biochemical analysis of the blood for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test were all within normal limits. The tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No lesions were observed on the upper endoscopy and the abdominal ultrasound.

No clinically apparent disease.description: The available information is most consistent with an asymptomatic person without an identified illness. The barium enema findings are not provided, so a specific gastrointestinal diagnosis cannot be established.

Constitutional thinness.description: A naturally low body weight without an underlying systemic illness. This is a possibility, but confirmation requires weight history, dietary assessment, and exclusion of other causes of underweight.

Asymptomatic colorectal adenoma.description: A benign glandular polyp with potential to develop into colorectal cancer. Small adenomas can be incidental screening findings, but no colorectal imaging result is supplied to support this diagnosis.

Colonic lipoma.description: A benign fatty tumor of the bowel wall that is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. Diagnosis requires characteristic imaging or endoscopic findings that are not provided here.

Asymptomatic colonic diverticulosis.description: Small outpouchings of the colonic wall that can be detected on barium enema without causing symptoms. This is less common at age 31 and cannot be inferred without the examination findings.

case: A 67-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 4-month history of dry cough, wheezing, and mild dyspnea that had initially been diagnosed as eosinophilic asthma at another hospital, with symptoms worsening despite treatment with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. He had no smoking history and unremarkable medical history. On examination, he required 1L nasal cannula oxygen with SaO2 of 96%, had decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung field with fine crackles, and no raised JVP, murmurs, gallop, or peripheral edema. Chest x-ray showed right ground glass opacities, and high-resolution CT revealed ground glass opacities surrounded by consolidation in the right lower lung field.

Organizing pneumonia.description: An inflammatory lung disorder in which granulation tissue fills small airways and alveoli. It may be cryptogenic or secondary to another condition. Ground-glass opacity surrounded by consolidation can represent the reverse halo sign, a supportive but nonspecific finding.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An inflammatory disorder involving eosinophil accumulation in lung tissue, often associated with asthma and usually producing peripheral pulmonary opacities. Blood or bronchoalveolar lavage eosinophilia would support the diagnosis.

Pneumonic-type lung adenocarcinoma.description: A lung adenocarcinoma growth pattern, often associated with invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma, that produces persistent consolidation or ground-glass opacities resembling pneumonia. It can occur in people who have never smoked.

Primary pulmonary lymphoma, particularly.normalized_text: Primary pulmonary lymphoma, particularly pulmonary MALT lymphoma
Primary pulmonary lymphoma, particularly.description: An uncommon, often indolent lymphoma involving the lung that can produce persistent consolidation, nodules, or ground-glass opacities with few systemic symptoms.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis.description: A fungal lung infection caused by Cryptococcus species that can affect immunocompetent people and occasionally produce consolidation, ground-glass opacities, or a reverse halo pattern.

case: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Crohn disease.description: A leading possibility: chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract. In children, growth failure, anemia, and systemic inflammation may precede prominent diarrhea.

Ulcerative colitis.description: Inflammatory bowel disease involving the colon, typically causing bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and anemia; severe disease can produce fever and growth impairment.

Intestinal amebiasis.description: Entamoeba histolytica infection can cause inflammatory colitis with abdominal pain and bloody stools after exposure in endemic regions, including the Caribbean.

Heavy Trichuris trichiura infection.description: Heavy whipworm infection can cause chronic inflammatory colitis, intestinal blood loss, iron-deficiency anemia, and impaired growth in children.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis involving the bowel or abdominal lymph nodes can cause chronic abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, anemia, and substantial inflammation, sometimes mimicking Crohn disease.

Celiac disease.description: An immune-mediated response to gluten that damages the small intestine and can cause malabsorption, growth failure, abdominal symptoms, and severe iron-deficiency anemia.

case: A 39-year-old man presented to the emergency department during the summer with a 4-day history of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, and fatigue following his return from a 2-week trip to East Africa. During his trip to Tanzania, he had been on safari without animal contact but received mosquito bites, especially during the first days. He consumed cooked shrimp and lobster and a small amount of raw tuna. On the second-to-last day of the trip, he developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. Upon returning to Massachusetts, he experienced fever (38.3°C to 39.5°C), shaking chills, diffuse headache, and lower back pain. He reported weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during fever episodes. His medical history included degenerative knee disease with previous glucocorticoid injections. On examination, he had a temperature of 38.9°C, blood pressure 113/62 mm Hg, facial flushing, mild scleral icterus, and dark brown urine.

Malaria, particularly Plasmodium falcipa.description: A mosquito-borne parasitic infection that can cause hemolysis, jaundice, and acute kidney injury. Fever after travel to Tanzania with dark urine and reduced urine output warrants urgent malaria testing and assessment for severe disease.

Leptospirosis with possible Weil disease.description: A bacterial infection acquired through water or soil contaminated with infected animal urine. Severe disease can cause jaundice and kidney failure; a relevant environmental exposure is not documented here.

Dengue.description: A mosquito-borne viral infection causing acute fever, headache, muscle pain, and sometimes gastrointestinal symptoms. Severe cases can involve liver injury, shock, or kidney injury.

Yellow fever.description: A mosquito-borne viral infection that can progress from a febrile illness to hepatitis, jaundice, bleeding, and kidney failure. Its likelihood depends on vaccination status and the exact itinerary; Tanzania generally has low potential for exposure.

Enteric fever, including typhoid or para.normalized_text: Enteric fever, including typhoid or paratyphoid fever
Enteric fever, including typhoid or para.description: A systemic Salmonella infection acquired through contaminated food or water. It can cause prolonged fever, headache, fatigue, and gastrointestinal illness after travel.

case: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

Extensive cervicothoracic paraspinal abs.description: A deep infection of tissues adjacent to the spine, directly supported by CT and MRI showing an abscess from C4 to T11. This extensive infection requires urgent specialist evaluation.

Delayed cervical spinal instrumentation.description: An infection involving implanted cervical stabilization hardware that can develop years after surgery and cause adjacent abscess formation.

Vertebral osteomyelitis with associated.normalized_text: Vertebral osteomyelitis with associated paraspinal abscess
Vertebral osteomyelitis with associated.description: Infection of vertebral bone, sometimes involving adjacent discs, that can spread into paraspinal tissues. Bone or disc involvement would need confirmation on imaging or tissue sampling.

Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess.normalized_text: Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess with spinal extension
Retropharyngeal or prevertebral abscess.description: A deep neck-space infection that can cause painful swallowing and spread into adjacent spinal tissues. The precise abscess compartment would need clarification from imaging.

Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation r.normalized_text: Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation related to cervical hardware
Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation r.description: A rare delayed complication in which cervical instrumentation erodes into the pharynx or esophagus, allowing contamination of deep cervical tissues and abscess formation. This is a possible underlying cause rather than an established finding.

case: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophage.description: A life-threatening full-thickness tear of the esophagus caused by a sudden pressure increase during forceful vomiting. This is a leading concern with severe chest pain following emesis; early laboratory results can be normal.

Acute coronary syndrome.description: Reduced blood flow to the heart causing unstable angina or myocardial infarction. An initially normal cardiac evaluation does not always exclude it, depending on the tests performed and their timing.

Acute aortic dissection.description: A life-threatening tear in the inner lining of the aorta that allows blood to separate the vessel wall layers, often causing severe chest pain radiating to the back.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas, typically producing persistent upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with nausea and vomiting. Diagnosis requires pancreatic enzyme testing and sometimes imaging.

Distal esophageal spasm.description: Abnormal, premature esophageal contractions that can cause severe noncardiac chest pain, often with difficulty swallowing. Dangerous causes of chest pain must be excluded first.

case: 27-year-old man with 2-year history of recurrent convulsive episodes. Initial events involved shaking of the trunk, arms, and legs lasting 4–5 minutes, preceded by occipital/neck pain, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Four months before admission, an episode occurred while drinking alcohol, with sudden body stiffening, backward fall, generalized shaking for 5–8 minutes, and urinary incontinence. Despite levetiracetam, seizures continued about weekly 3 months before admission. One month before admission, he was found on the floor with shaking and clenching movements lasting about 2 minutes. On examination, he was awake and alert but mute, with a stiff posture and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs. He had extensive burn scars on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. Past history included febrile seizure in childhood, several concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. Family history was notable for maternal schizoaffective disorder and post-traumatic epilepsy. Laboratory studies were largely normal, with mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

Functional seizures (psychogenic nonepil.description: Involuntary seizure-like episodes caused by altered nervous-system functioning rather than epileptic electrical activity. This is a leading consideration, but diagnosis requires clinical assessment and ideally video-EEG capture of typical episodes; psychiatric history alone is not diagnostic.

Epilepsy with bilateral tonic-clonic sei.normalized_text: Epilepsy with bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, possibly focal onset
Epilepsy with bilateral tonic-clonic sei.description: A disorder of recurrent seizures from abnormal brain electrical activity. Autonomic or visual symptoms can precede focal seizures that progress to bilateral convulsions.

Convulsive syncope.description: Transient loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain, sometimes accompanied by stiffening and brief jerking. Reflex-mediated syncope and cardiac arrhythmias are potential causes.

Panic attacks with dissociative symptoms.description: Episodes of intense autonomic arousal that may include shaking, nausea, palpitations, visual disturbance, and impaired concentration. Dissociative symptoms may coexist, particularly with trauma-related disorders.

Catatonia.description: A psychomotor syndrome associated with psychiatric or medical illness, characterized by findings such as mutism, posturing, rigidity, and abnormal motor activity. It could explain aspects of the examination but would not readily explain the entire episodic history.

case: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.normalized_text: Incarcerated right obturator hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.description: Bowel becomes trapped in the obturator canal, potentially compromising its blood supply. This is the leading diagnosis and requires urgent surgical assessment. It classically affects thin, elderly, multiparous women and can cause referred knee pain through obturator nerve compression.

Incarcerated right femoral hernia causin.normalized_text: Incarcerated right femoral hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated right femoral hernia causin.description: Bowel becomes trapped in the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. Femoral hernias occur disproportionately in older women and can cause acute obstruction or strangulation.

Incarcerated right sciatic hernia causin.normalized_text: Incarcerated right sciatic hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated right sciatic hernia causin.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through a sciatic foramen, potentially causing obstruction and pain from nearby nerve compression.

Pelvic malignancy causing small-bowel ob.description: A pelvic tumor can obstruct small bowel through direct compression, invasion, or peritoneal spread and may cause referred leg pain if it involves pelvic nerves.

Internal pelvic hernia causing small-bow.normalized_text: Internal pelvic hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Internal pelvic hernia causing small-bow.description: Bowel becomes trapped through an internal pelvic defect, such as a broad-ligament defect. Such hernias can cause acute obstruction even without previous abdominal surgery.

case: 23-year-old Korean female with 6 months of recurrent bilateral visual field defects and headache, worsened 1 month before presentation. She presented with 1 day of left eye visual disturbance and left visual field defect, then developed sudden left-sided hearing loss 2 days later. Three weeks after initial presentation, she reported right eye visual field defect, and 2 days later was admitted for tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. She denied diabetes, hypertension, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, hematologic or cardiovascular disease, oral contraceptive use, and pregnancy. Initial exam showed reactive pupils without RAPD, visual acuity 20/20 OD and 20/25 OS, normal intraocular pressures, and normal anterior segment findings. Laboratory tests were normal, and CSF showed mildly elevated protein without oligoclonal bands.

Susac syndrome.description: An immune-mediated microangiopathy affecting the retina, brain, and inner ear, classically causing branch retinal artery occlusions, neurological symptoms, and sensorineural hearing loss. This is the leading consideration, although retinal angiography, brain MRI, and audiometry are needed for confirmation.

Multiple sclerosis.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can produce relapsing visual, sensory, and other neurological deficits.

Cogan syndrome.description: A rare inflammatory disorder combining ocular inflammation, classically interstitial keratitis, with inner-ear dysfunction causing hearing loss, tinnitus, and sometimes vertigo.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: An inflammatory disease of cerebral blood vessels that can cause headache and recurrent focal neurological deficits. Retinal and inner-ear involvement would be less characteristic than in Susac syndrome.

Migraine with aura.description: A neurological disorder producing recurrent headaches with reversible visual or sensory symptoms. It may explain some episodes but does not adequately account for the entire presentation.

case: 73-year-old woman with a 10-year history of severe paraspinal muscle atrophy and cerebellar ataxia. Symptoms began at age 63 with mild stooping posture, then progressed to gait instability requiring a walking stick by age 68 and difficulty climbing stairs by age 70. Exam showed moderate neck flexion weakness, mild proximal limb weakness, poor tandem gait balance without limb ataxia, and MMSE 25. History also included sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss and frequent premature contractions on Holter monitoring. Labs showed elevated CK, normal resting blood and CSF lactate, slightly low TSH, elevated antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, elevated rheumatoid factor, and mildly positive ANA. Needle EMG of biceps brachii and rectus femoris showed mild myopathic features.

Mitochondrial myopathy with multisystem.description: A mitochondrial energy-production disorder that can cause axial and proximal muscle weakness, cerebellar dysfunction, hearing loss, and cardiac abnormalities. Normal resting blood and CSF lactate do not exclude it.

Myofibrillar myopathy.description: A group of muscle protein-aggregation disorders that may present in later adulthood with axial or proximal weakness and, in some subtypes, cardiac conduction abnormalities or cardiomyopathy.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: An inherited acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causing lysosomal glycogen accumulation, often producing axial and limb-girdle weakness with prominent respiratory muscle involvement.

Sporadic inclusion body myositis.description: A slowly progressive muscle disease of older adults, typically affecting quadriceps and finger flexors; axial weakness can occur but is an uncommon dominant presentation.

Immune-mediated axial myopathy.description: An inflammatory muscle disorder predominantly affecting spinal extensor muscles, potentially causing progressive bent-spine posture, muscle atrophy, and elevated CK. Autoimmune serologies may suggest an autoimmune background but do not establish this diagnosis.

case: A 2-year-old Korean male was admitted for evaluation and management of left hip pain. Physical examination revealed several palpable lymph nodes in the left inguinal area and an ill-defined heterogeneous mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle. Peripheral blood examination showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.83 × 10^9/L, platelet count 182 × 10^9/L, and 5 atypical lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells. Immunophenotyping of neoplastic cells showed positivity for CD45 (99.0%), CD19 (94.84%), CD10 (27.64%), CD20 (94.24%), HLA-DR (95.70%), surface IgG lambda (96.45%), CD13 (22.46%), and CD117 (22.22%), and negativity for CD34 (0.01%), Tdt (0.64%), myeloperoxidase (0.01%), and various T-cell and myeloid markers.

diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma that can involve lymph nodes and extranodal tissues, including skeletal muscle. The strong CD19 and CD20 expression, monotypic surface IgG lambda, and absence of TdT and CD34 favor a mature B-cell malignancy. Confirmation requires tissue morphology and additional studies.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A rapidly growing mature germinal-center B-cell lymphoma affecting children, usually associated with a MYC rearrangement. Tissue morphology, proliferation index, and MYC testing are needed to distinguish it from other aggressive B-cell lymphomas.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with high-grade morphology that does not meet criteria for a more specific entity. This diagnosis requires biopsy and genetic studies and cannot be established from immunophenotyping alone.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.description: A malignancy of immature B-cell precursors that commonly affects young children and may cause anemia, musculoskeletal pain, lymphadenopathy, or tissue masses. The reported mature surface immunoglobulin phenotype makes this substantially less likely.

Pediatric-type follicular lymphoma.description: A usually localized mature germinal-center B-cell lymphoma occurring predominantly in boys. It typically presents as nodal disease and requires demonstration of follicular architecture on biopsy.

case: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni. An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.

Intestinal schistosomiasis with possible.normalized_text: Intestinal schistosomiasis with possible hepatic involvement
Intestinal schistosomiasis with possible.description: Schistosoma mansoni infection is established by eggs in the stool. It can cause chronic intestinal inflammation and hepatic granulomatous disease, although imaging is needed to assess liver involvement.

Pyogenic liver abscess associated with s.normalized_text: Pyogenic liver abscess associated with schistosomiasis
Pyogenic liver abscess associated with s.description: A bacterial collection within the liver can cause prolonged fever and focal pain. Schistosomal liver lesions may predispose to bacterial seeding, making this a possible complication rather than an alternative to the documented infection.

Amoebic liver abscess with concurrent sc.normalized_text: Amoebic liver abscess with concurrent schistosomiasis
Amoebic liver abscess with concurrent sc.description: Entamoeba histolytica can spread from the intestine to the liver and produce an abscess. Demonstration of Schistosoma mansoni does not exclude a second intestinal infection.

Infected post-traumatic hepatic hematoma.description: Liver injury following abdominal trauma can produce a hematoma that subsequently becomes infected, causing persistent fever and right upper quadrant pain.

Enteric fever with concurrent schistosom.description: Systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi can produce sustained fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhoea; hepatic involvement can occasionally cause right upper quadrant discomfort.

case: 44-year-old man with 1 month of intermittent nonexertional substernal burning chest pain, lasting hours to days and temporarily relieved by antacids/omeprazole, now presenting with a severe episode radiating to the left arm that woke him from sleep 1 hour prior and was associated with nausea and nonbloody vomiting. He denied dyspnea, edema, fever, cough, trauma, or immobility. Past history was otherwise unremarkable, though he recalled being told 12 years earlier that his platelet count was about 600,000/mm³; he also reported intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers, without bleeding, thrombosis, erythromelalgia, headache, dizziness, or other neurologic symptoms. On exam he was afebrile, in distress clutching his chest, with regular cardiac rhythm, no JVD or edema, normal lung exam, and nontender abdomen/chest. Labs showed leukocytosis (22,000/mm³ with neutrophilia and bandemia), thrombocytosis (771,000/mm³), hemoglobin 17.5 g/dL, glucose 192 mg/dL, and troponin 0.08 ng/mL.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute coronary syndrome, including possi.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome, including possible acute myocardial infarction
Acute coronary syndrome, including possi.description: Acute myocardial ischemia, often caused by coronary thrombosis. The current episode requires emergency evaluation with ECG and serial troponins; an underlying myeloproliferative disorder could increase thrombotic risk.

Essential thrombocythemia with possible.normalized_text: Essential thrombocythemia with possible coronary thrombosis
Essential thrombocythemia with possible.description: A clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by persistent thrombocytosis and increased arterial and venous thrombotic risk. Diagnosis requires molecular testing, bone marrow assessment, and exclusion of reactive thrombocytosis and other myeloproliferative neoplasms.

Polycythemia vera with possible coronary.normalized_text: Polycythemia vera with possible coronary thrombosis
Polycythemia vera with possible coronary.description: A usually JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasm causing increased red cell production, often with leukocytosis and thrombocytosis. Aquagenic pruritus and thrombosis are characteristic; the hemoglobin warrants evaluation but is not diagnostic alone.

Vasospastic angina.description: Transient coronary artery spasm causing ischemic chest pain, commonly at rest or overnight. Prolonged spasm can cause myocardial injury, but ECG documentation and coronary evaluation are needed.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease.description: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus causing retrosternal burning, sometimes worse while recumbent. It could explain earlier symptoms but must not be used to dismiss the current potentially ischemic episode.

case: Newborn girl admitted to the NICU after cardiorespiratory arrest at delivery. Born at 40 weeks by cesarean section for nonreassuring fetal status after 22 hours 39 minutes of labor; meconium-stained fluid and breech delivery. Prenatal course notable for right-sided urinary tract dilatation on serial ultrasound, maternal hepatitis C infection, treated Chlamydia trachomatis infection, and gestational hypertension. At birth she was limp with no respiratory effort; required 16 minutes of resuscitation including intubation, CPR, epinephrine, and saline boluses before spontaneous circulation returned. Apgar scores were 1, 0, 0, 1, and 3 at 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes. On NICU admission, temperature was 34.9°C, heart rate 141 bpm, blood pressure 84/59 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97% on mechanical ventilation. Therapeutic hypothermia was started.

Severe perinatal asphyxia with suspected.normalized_text: Severe perinatal asphyxia with suspected hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Severe perinatal asphyxia with suspected.description: Inadequate oxygen delivery and blood flow around birth can cause profound cardiorespiratory depression and brain injury. This is the leading concern, although encephalopathy severity requires neurologic examination, EEG, and other testing.

Meconium aspiration syndrome.description: Aspiration of meconium-contaminated amniotic fluid can cause airway obstruction, lung inflammation, and severe respiratory failure, sometimes complicated by pulmonary hypertension.

Early-onset neonatal sepsis or congenita.normalized_text: Early-onset neonatal sepsis or congenital pneumonia
Early-onset neonatal sepsis or congenita.description: Infection acquired before or during delivery can cause respiratory failure, circulatory collapse, and depressed neonatal responsiveness. Maternal fever, membrane-rupture duration, cultures, and inflammatory markers are not provided.

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the.normalized_text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the.description: Failure of pulmonary vascular resistance to fall after birth causes right-to-left shunting and hypoxemic respiratory failure. It can complicate perinatal asphyxia or meconium aspiration and requires echocardiographic assessment.

Birth-related intracranial hemorrhage.description: Intracranial bleeding associated with delivery trauma or severe hypoxic injury can cause neurologic depression, apnea, and cardiovascular instability. Neuroimaging is needed for diagnosis.

case: 54-year-old man with polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. He was afebrile, drowsy, and hypertensive, with distended jugular veins and bibasilar crackles. History included a sister with renal failure of unclear cause requiring dialysis at age 45. Labs showed severe renal dysfunction (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), mild anemia, proteinuria with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 1.9, rare schistocytes on blood film, elevated LDH, and low C3 with normal C4 that persisted during hospitalization. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine and metabolites. Cultures were negative. Ultrasound showed echogenic kidneys measuring 9.8 cm and 10.3 cm.

Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.normalized_text: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome)
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.description: Dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway causes small-vessel endothelial injury, predominantly affecting the kidneys. Inherited susceptibility may be unmasked by triggers such as cocaine use or severe hypertension.

C3 glomerulopathy.description: A complement-mediated glomerular disease, including C3 glomerulonephritis and dense deposit disease, caused by abnormal alternative complement pathway activity. Diagnosis requires kidney biopsy.

Cocaine-associated hypertensive kidney i.normalized_text: Cocaine-associated hypertensive kidney injury with secondary thrombotic microangiopathy
Cocaine-associated hypertensive kidney i.description: Cocaine can cause marked vasoconstriction and severe hypertension, leading to renal vascular injury and secondary thrombotic microangiopathy.

Hepatitis C-associated cryoglobulinemic.description: Hepatitis C can cause circulating cryoglobulin-containing immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli, usually producing a membranoproliferative pattern of injury.

Infection-related glomerulonephritis.description: Glomerular inflammation associated with an active or recent infection can cause complement consumption, proteinuria, hypertension, and acute kidney injury.

Advanced chronic kidney disease due to h.normalized_text: Advanced chronic kidney disease due to hypertensive nephrosclerosis
Advanced chronic kidney disease due to h.description: Chronic hypertensive vascular injury can cause progressive kidney scarring, proteinuria, and eventual kidney failure with uremic encephalopathy and fluid overload.

case: 44-year-old Chinese woman, previously healthy, with a 7-week history of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting and 13 kg weight loss. She denied abdominal pain, distension, or diarrhea. Initial treatment for presumed functional gastrointestinal disorder, including antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics, was ineffective. Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, loss of pharyngeal reflex, decreased tendon reflexes on the right, and bilateral Babinski sign. Prior gastroscopy and abdominal CT were normal.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder w.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder with area postrema and brainstem involvement
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder w.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder, often associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies. Area postrema involvement can cause persistent nausea and vomiting before other neurological deficits appear. This is the leading diagnostic consideration; brain MRI and serum aquaporin-4 IgG testing would help evaluate it.

Brainstem neoplasm involving the dorsal.normalized_text: Brainstem neoplasm involving the dorsal medulla
Brainstem neoplasm involving the dorsal.description: A tumor involving medullary emetic centers, cranial nerve nuclei, and motor pathways can produce progressive vomiting followed by focal neurological deficits and respiratory compromise.

Posterior circulation ischemic stroke in.normalized_text: Posterior circulation ischemic stroke involving the medulla
Posterior circulation ischemic stroke in.description: Brainstem ischemia can impair vestibular, bulbar, respiratory, and motor pathways, causing vomiting, nystagmus, swallowing-related reflex abnormalities, weakness, and respiratory failure.

Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to pro.normalized_text: Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to prolonged vomiting
Wernicke encephalopathy secondary to pro.description: Thiamine deficiency from severe nutritional depletion can cause ocular motor abnormalities, ataxia, and altered mental status. It could complicate the prolonged vomiting but would not adequately explain its original cause.

Inflammatory or infectious rhombencephal.description: Inflammation of the brainstem and cerebellum, caused by infection or immune-mediated disease, can produce asymmetric cranial nerve deficits, long-tract signs, and respiratory compromise.

case: 47-year-old male with 2-month history of fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. History of inguinal hernia repair surgery 10 years ago and cardiac disease. On admission, body temperature was 37.3°C. Physical examination revealed aortic valve diastolic murmurs at the precordium.

Subacute bacterial infective endocarditi.description: An infection of the heart valves, often caused by viridans streptococci or enterococci, that can develop gradually over weeks to months. Prolonged constitutional symptoms and an aortic diastolic murmur warrant prompt blood cultures and echocardiography.

Q fever endocarditis.description: Persistent heart-valve infection caused by Coxiella burnetii, particularly in patients with preexisting valvular disease. Routine blood cultures are usually negative; exposure history and specific testing help establish the diagnosis.

Brucella endocarditis.description: A rare complication of brucellosis that frequently involves the aortic valve. Contact with infected livestock or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products would strengthen this possibility.

Bartonella endocarditis.description: A typically culture-negative heart-valve infection caused by Bartonella species. Cat exposure, body-louse exposure, or certain housing-related risks can provide important diagnostic clues.

Tropheryma whipplei endocarditis.description: A rare, typically culture-negative valve infection associated with the organism that causes Whipple disease. It can occur in middle-aged men with arthralgia even without gastrointestinal symptoms.

case: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.

Paradoxical systemic air embolism throug.normalized_text: Paradoxical systemic air embolism through a patent foramen ovale
Paradoxical systemic air embolism throug.description: Venous air introduced during venesection can cross a patent foramen ovale into the arterial circulation, causing cerebral and coronary embolization. This is the most unifying explanation for this presentation and is a medical emergency.

Venous air embolism with pulmonary vascu.normalized_text: Venous air embolism with pulmonary vascular obstruction
Venous air embolism with pulmonary vascu.description: Air entering the venous circulation can obstruct pulmonary blood flow, producing acute hypoxemia, dyspnoea, and chest pain. An associated right-to-left shunt permits systemic air embolization.

Acute coronary syndrome due to atheroscl.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to atherosclerotic plaque rupture
Acute coronary syndrome due to atheroscl.description: Acute coronary thrombosis can cause myocardial ischemia or infarction, with typical anginal pain, ECG abnormalities, and elevated troponin.

Pulmonary thromboembolism with paradoxic.normalized_text: Pulmonary thromboembolism with paradoxical cerebral embolism
Pulmonary thromboembolism with paradoxic.description: A venous thrombus can embolize to the lungs and, if it crosses a patent foramen ovale, to the cerebral circulation. This can produce simultaneous respiratory distress and focal neurological deficits.

Acute aortic dissection with coronary an.normalized_text: Acute aortic dissection with coronary and cerebral malperfusion
Acute aortic dissection with coronary an.description: A tear in the aortic wall can compromise coronary and cerebral arterial flow, causing abrupt chest pain, myocardial injury, and focal neurological deficits.

case: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), CNS.description: An astrocytic tumor that often arises superficially in the cerebral hemispheres of young people and presents with seizures. BRAF V600E mutations are common. This is the established diagnosis based on the reported biopsy/resection pathology.

Ganglioglioma.description: A usually slow-growing glioneuronal tumor frequently associated with longstanding seizures in young patients. BRAF V600E mutations can occur, making it a differential consideration, but the reported histopathology supports PXA instead.

Pilocytic astrocytoma.description: A generally slow-growing astrocytic tumor occurring predominantly in children and young adults. It can resemble PXA histologically and occasionally carries BRAF V600E, although other MAPK-pathway alterations are more typical. The reported pathology does not establish this diagnosis.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, with epithel.description: An aggressive astrocytic malignancy that can harbor BRAF V600E and overlap morphologically with PXA. It is substantially less consistent with the reported WHO grade 2 pathology and prolonged clinical course; no malignant progression is documented.

case: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous and erythematous rash involving the eyelids, elbows, knuckles, knees, and fingertips, followed 1 week later by intense generalized myalgias and progressive proximal muscle weakness with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Exam showed heliotrope rash, periungual edema/erythema, erythematous papules on the extensor fingers, elbows, and knees, pitting edema of the limbs, diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, hypoactive bowel sounds, and marked weakness of the deltoids, triceps, hip flexors, hamstrings, and quadriceps; sensation, reflexes, muscle bulk, and tone were normal. He was afebrile but tachycardic, tachypneic, mildly hypoxemic on oxygen, with reduced limb and neck strength. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier.

Dermatomyositis with generalized edema.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive skin lesions. Severe edematous dermatomyositis best explains this presentation; respiratory muscle weakness or pulmonary involvement may contribute to hypoxemia.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: An autoimmune syndrome involving inflammatory myopathy, interstitial lung disease, and variably arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and roughened fingertips called mechanic's hands. Some patients have dermatomyositis-type skin findings.

Connective tissue disease-associated ove.description: Inflammatory muscle disease occurring alongside another systemic autoimmune disorder, such as systemic sclerosis or mixed connective tissue disease. Pulmonary and gastrointestinal involvement can accompany weakness.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: An autoimmune myopathy causing muscle fiber necrosis and often severe, rapidly progressive proximal and neck weakness. Characteristic inflammatory skin lesions are usually absent.

Polymyositis.description: A rare inflammatory myopathy causing subacute symmetric proximal weakness without the characteristic rash of dermatomyositis. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is substantially less likely here because of the skin findings.

case: A 59-year-old woman presented with a longstanding history of epilepsy with complex partial seizures, for which she had been using phenytoin for more than 20 years. She was referred with a 3-year history of progressive muscle weakness, associated with generalized bone and muscle pain, resulting in significant limitations in her daily activities. Her symptoms had further worsened with progressive proximal muscle pain and weakness and increasing bone pain. Physical examination revealed normal renal and liver function. Conventional radiographs demonstrated Looser's zones in the femoral neck bilaterally.

Phenytoin-induced vitamin D deficiency o.description: The most likely diagnosis. Long-term phenytoin use accelerates vitamin D breakdown, impairing bone mineralization and causing bone pain, proximal weakness, and Looser's zones (pseudofractures).

Hypophosphatemic osteomalacia.description: Defective bone mineralization caused by chronic phosphate depletion, sometimes due to renal phosphate wasting or an FGF23-secreting tumor. Renal phosphate wasting can occur despite normal overall renal function.

Primary hyperparathyroidism with skeleta.description: Excess parathyroid hormone secretion causes increased bone turnover and can produce skeletal pain, fragility fractures, and proximal muscle weakness.

Postmenopausal osteoporosis with insuffi.description: Reduced bone mass increases fracture risk in postmenopausal women; long-term antiseizure medication use can contribute to skeletal fragility.

Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy.description: An autoimmune muscle disorder causing progressive, usually symmetric proximal weakness and sometimes muscle pain.

case: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

Group A streptococcal infective endocard.normalized_text: Group A streptococcal infective endocarditis, likely involving the mitral valve
Group A streptococcal infective endocard.description: Bacterial infection of the cardiac endocardium or valves. This is the leading unifying diagnosis: mitral valve involvement could cause regurgitation and heart failure, while infected emboli could cause an acute cerebral infarction. Urgent echocardiography and brain imaging are needed.

Acute ischemic stroke, potentially cause.normalized_text: Acute ischemic stroke, potentially caused by a septic cardiac embolus
Acute ischemic stroke, potentially cause.description: Sudden interruption of cerebral blood flow causing focal neurological deficits. In this case, an embolus from an infected heart valve is a concerning potential cause.

Acute decompensated heart failure due to.normalized_text: Acute decompensated heart failure due to significant mitral regurgitation
Acute decompensated heart failure due to.description: Backward flow through an incompetent mitral valve can cause pulmonary congestion and respiratory distress. Infective endocarditis could precipitate acute deterioration through valve damage.

Group A streptococcal sepsis with enceph.normalized_text: Group A streptococcal sepsis with encephalopathy and possible myocardial dysfunction
Group A streptococcal sepsis with enceph.description: Systemic infection causing organ dysfunction, potentially including altered mental status, respiratory compromise, and impaired cardiac performance. Endocarditis must be investigated as a possible source.

Acute myocarditis associated with strept.normalized_text: Acute myocarditis associated with streptococcal infection
Acute myocarditis associated with strept.description: Inflammation of the myocardium that can cause ventricular dysfunction and heart failure. This is less likely than infective endocarditis given the bacteremia, prominent apical murmur, and focal neurological deficits.

case: Patient 1: 3.5-year-old male from unrelated Polish parents. Born at 39 weeks gestation with birth weight 3700g (50th-75th centile), length 57cm (97th centile), head circumference 36cm (75th-97th centile), thorax circumference 33cm (25-50th centile), Apgar score 9 at 1 min. Family history unremarkable. Proteinuria, hematuria and glycosuria noted in early neonatal period. UTI at 12 months. At 3 years developed bronchopneumonia with elevated creatinine. Laboratory investigations showed constant proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, eGFR (Schwartz) 30.56 ml/min/1.73 m2, elevated serum creatinine, uric acid, urea, total cholesterol, and triglyceride; normal CBC, blood glucose, albumin, thyroid and liver function tests. Renal ultrasound showed increased cortex echogenicity and decreased corticomedullary differentiation. Normal male karyotype (46,XY).

Dent disease type 1 (CLCN5-related).description: An X-linked proximal renal tubular disorder causing low-molecular-weight proteinuria, often with hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and progressive kidney dysfunction. Urinary protein characterization, urine calcium measurement, and genetic testing help establish the diagnosis.

Dent disease type 2 (OCRL-related).description: An X-linked OCRL-associated proximal tubulopathy characterized by low-molecular-weight proteinuria and variable glycosuria, hypercalciuria, and kidney dysfunction. Unlike classic Lowe syndrome, prominent eye and neurological abnormalities may be absent.

Infantile nephropathic cystinosis.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal cystine-storage disorder causing proximal tubular Fanconi syndrome and progressive chronic kidney disease. Leukocyte cystine measurement and CTNS testing are diagnostic investigations.

HNF1B-associated kidney disease.description: A genetic developmental kidney disorder that can cause echogenic or dysplastic kidneys, tubular dysfunction, hyperuricemia, and childhood chronic kidney disease. Diabetes and other extrarenal manifestations may develop later or remain absent.

Mitochondrial disease with renal proxima.normalized_text: Mitochondrial disease with renal proximal tubulopathy
Mitochondrial disease with renal proxima.description: Mitochondrial energy-production defects can impair proximal tubular transport, producing Fanconi-type urinary losses and progressive kidney dysfunction. Some affected children initially have predominantly renal disease.

case: A 58-year-old man presented with a six-week history of muscle weakness, dysphagia, and a symmetrical widespread rash on the face, torso, and limbs. Laboratory testing revealed elevated creatine kinase of 7070 u/L (reference range 30-175). An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed and showed abnormal findings, and a PET CT scan was arranged.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by muscle weakness and characteristic skin eruptions. Swallowing muscles may be involved. This is the strongest fit, although rash morphology and further testing are needed for confirmation.

Malignancy-associated dermatomyositis.description: Dermatomyositis occurring in association with an underlying malignancy. New-onset disease at age 58 warrants cancer evaluation; abnormal endoscopy may be relevant, but neither it nor a planned PET CT establishes malignancy.

Overlap myositis.description: Inflammatory muscle disease associated with another connective tissue disorder, such as systemic sclerosis, lupus, or mixed connective tissue disease. It can combine muscle inflammation, skin disease, and swallowing dysfunction.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: An autoimmune myopathy causing prominent muscle fiber injury, substantial creatine kinase elevation, and often severe weakness. It may be associated with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies.

Polymyositis.description: A rare inflammatory myopathy causing symmetrical muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes, sometimes with swallowing impairment. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and ordinarily lacks a characteristic rash.

case: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, most commonly boys aged 4–10 years. This is the leading consideration, although the radiographic findings are not provided.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A temporary inflammatory condition of the hip that commonly causes pain and limping in otherwise well children, sometimes following a viral illness.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis.description: Displacement of the femoral head through the growth plate, usually occurring in adolescents; presentation at age 8 is uncommon and may warrant evaluation for an underlying endocrine disorder.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: A bacterial infection of the hip joint requiring urgent evaluation and treatment. It usually causes acute severe pain, fever, and marked difficulty bearing weight, although fever may occasionally be absent.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis.description: Chronic inflammatory arthritis beginning before age 16 that can cause persistent joint pain, stiffness, and restricted movement. Isolated hip involvement at presentation is less common.

case: A 62-year-old fit and well Romanian man presented with a two-week history of worsening acute localized pain in the upper abdomen and vomiting. His surgical history included an open appendectomy as a child and laparoscopic cholecystectomy 20 years ago. On presentation, he had fever (39°C) and tachycardia (104 beats/min), with blood pressure of 125/73 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, worse in the right upper quadrant, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 16 × 10⁹/L (reference range 4-10 × 10⁹/L) and a C reactive protein concentration of 277 mg/L (reference value <9 mg/L). A frontal projection erect chest radiograph was initially reported as showing pneumoperitoneum, but showed a normal bowel gas pattern under the left hemidiaphragm.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial infection forming a pus-filled cavity in the liver. Gas within an abscess near the liver dome can mimic free air beneath the diaphragm on a chest radiograph.

Perforated peptic ulcer.description: A gastric or duodenal ulcer that perforates the gastrointestinal wall, potentially releasing air and digestive contents into the peritoneal cavity.

Right subphrenic abscess.description: An infected collection between the liver and diaphragm, sometimes containing gas that can resemble pneumoperitoneum.

Complicated Chilaiditi syndrome.description: Symptomatic interposition of bowel between the liver and right hemidiaphragm, which can mimic pneumoperitoneum. Associated obstruction, volvulus, or ischemia can produce severe illness.

Secondarily infected hepatic hydatid cys.description: A liver cyst caused by Echinococcus infection that becomes bacterially infected or ruptures. Romanian origin makes exposure epidemiologically plausible but does not establish infection.

case: A 1-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted for evaluation of psychomotor retardation and an operation for exotropia. She was born at term (gestational age: 40 weeks) by cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, and was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The family history was unremarkable. On admission, she presented with a characteristic high-pitched cry and microcephaly. She showed delayed motor functions and crawling, was able to sit unassisted but unable to stand, with developmental characteristics lagging behind for normal chronologic age. On neurologic examination, she had left leg hypotonia, with normal tendon reflexes and normal cranial nerve signs. When she was 6 months old, ventricular septal defect was detected by echocardiography. Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (5) (p15.2) one month after delivery.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, characterized by a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, hypotonia, and developmental delay. The documented 46,XX,del(5)(p15.2) establishes this diagnosis.

case: 7-year-old girl with no past medical history presented with intermittent abdominal pain for about 1 month, not relieved by anti-inflammatory treatment. Abdominal CT showed peritoneal effusion and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was elevated at 1,210 ng/mL. Ultrasound showed multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal hypoechoic lymph nodes. The bilateral ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina were unremarkable. Surgical resection revealed a 4 cm full-thickness jejunal mass with grey-white cut surface; lymph nodes showed reactive hyperplasia.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.normalized_text: Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of the jejunum
Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.description: A malignant germ cell tumor with yolk sac differentiation that produces alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). A primary jejunal location is exceptionally rare, but this is the leading consideration given the elevated AFP and normal pelvic organs. Confirmation requires histopathology and immunohistochemistry.

Extragonadal mixed germ cell tumor with.normalized_text: Extragonadal mixed germ cell tumor with a yolk sac component
Extragonadal mixed germ cell tumor with.description: A malignant tumor containing multiple germ cell tumor components. A yolk sac component could explain AFP production, although a primary intestinal mixed germ cell tumor is exceptionally rare.

AFP-producing hepatoid adenocarcinoma of.normalized_text: AFP-producing hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the jejunum
AFP-producing hepatoid adenocarcinoma of.description: An exceptionally rare intestinal carcinoma with liver-like differentiation that may secrete AFP. Histology is needed to distinguish it from a yolk sac tumor.

Primary intestinal lymphoma, particularl.normalized_text: Primary intestinal lymphoma, particularly Burkitt lymphoma
Primary intestinal lymphoma, particularl.description: An aggressive lymphoid malignancy that can involve the small intestine in children, producing abdominal masses, pain, lymphadenopathy, and ascites.

Jejunal gastrointestinal stromal tumor.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal wall that can cause abdominal pain and a solid bowel mass. Pediatric cases are rare and usually arise in the stomach rather than the jejunum.

case: 6-month-old boy with 2 days of intermittent nocturnal abdominal pain causing crying, legs drawn to chest, and a rigid abdomen during episodes, followed by gastrointestinal bleeding with three stools of increasing reddish discoloration, the last nearly all blood with a large clot. History of infantile colic and gastroesophageal reflux treated with ranitidine; recently started pureed foods. Exam showed diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right, later pallor; no abdominal mass or anal fissure. Initial vitals: T 36.5°C, HR 178/min, BP 95/52 mmHg, RR 24/min, O2 sat 100%; later HR 168/min, BP 94/36 mmHg.

Ileocolic intussusception.description: Telescoping of one segment of intestine into another, causing obstruction and potentially bowel ischemia. This is the leading concern in this infant and requires emergency evaluation.

Bleeding Meckel diverticulum, potentiall.normalized_text: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum, potentially complicated by intussusception
Bleeding Meckel diverticulum, potentiall.description: A congenital small-intestinal pouch that may contain acid-producing gastric tissue and cause intestinal ulceration and bleeding. It can also serve as a lead point for intussusception.

Intestinal malrotation with midgut volvu.description: Abnormal intestinal rotation allows the bowel to twist around its blood supply, causing obstruction and ischemia. This is a surgical emergency.

Enteric duplication cyst with bleeding o.normalized_text: Enteric duplication cyst with bleeding or secondary intussusception
Enteric duplication cyst with bleeding o.description: A congenital cyst or duplicated intestinal segment that can cause obstruction, act as an intussusception lead point, or bleed when it contains ectopic gastric tissue.

Acute infectious colitis.description: Inflammation of the colon due to an intestinal infection, particularly invasive bacteria, which can cause abdominal cramps and bloody stools.

Food protein-induced allergic proctocoli.description: A non-IgE-mediated reaction to dietary proteins that causes distal intestinal inflammation and blood in the stools, typically in otherwise well infants.

case: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)
Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocr.description: A rare proliferation of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells, typically affecting older nonsmoking women, that can cause constrictive bronchiolitis and progressive airflow obstruction.

Constrictive bronchiolitis (bronchioliti.description: Fibrotic narrowing of small airways causing persistent airflow obstruction. It may be idiopathic or associated with autoimmune disease, inhalational injury, infection, transplantation, or medications.

Late-onset asthma with persistent airflo.normalized_text: Late-onset asthma with persistent airflow obstruction
