Late-onset asthma with persistent airflo.description: Inflammatory airway disease that can begin in adulthood and, when severe or associated with airway remodeling, produce substantial persistent airflow limitation.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a never-smoker
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in.description: Persistent airflow obstruction caused by small airway disease and sometimes emphysema. Although usually associated with smoking, it can occur with environmental exposures, impaired lung development, or genetic susceptibility.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with promin.normalized_text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with prominent small airway involvement
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with promin.description: An immune-mediated lung disease caused by inhaled antigens that can involve both lung tissue and small airways, sometimes producing substantial airflow obstruction.

case: 27-year-old man, previously healthy, with a few days of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. History notable for left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement since age 15, with intermittent spontaneous enlargement and shrinkage. On exam he was thin (168 cm, 48 kg), had a temperature of 37.6°C, oxygen saturation of 94% on room air, crackles in the left upper lung field, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis (WBC 20,000/μL) with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble interleukin-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures for bacteria, acid-fast organisms, and fungi were negative; ANCA, rheumatoid factor, HIV, and tumor markers were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identifiable pathogens.

Sarcoidosis with pulmonary and periphera.normalized_text: Sarcoidosis with pulmonary and peripheral lymph node involvement
Sarcoidosis with pulmonary and periphera.description: A systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by granulomas, commonly involving the lungs and lymph nodes. Diagnosis requires compatible pathology and exclusion of infection and other granulomatous diseases; the reported biopsy alone is not diagnostic.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with tuberculous.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause granulomatous pulmonary disease and cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Negative sputum cultures and absence of organisms on biopsy reduce support but do not completely exclude infection.

Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvem.normalized_text: Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvement or an associated granulomatous reaction
Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvem.description: A lymphoid malignancy that often presents in young adults with painless lymphadenopathy. Pulmonary involvement or associated sarcoid-like granulomatous inflammation can occur, but diagnosis requires appropriate lymph node tissue examination.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing granulomatous small-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys. ANCA-negative disease occurs, particularly when disease is localized.

Pulmonary histoplasmosis.description: A fungal infection acquired through inhalation of Histoplasma spores that can cause pulmonary granulomas and lymphadenopathy. Its likelihood depends substantially on geographic and environmental exposure, which was not provided.

case: A 31-year-old Caucasian man with multiple sclerosis who had received 24 natalizumab infusions and was switched to fingolimod due to persistent high anti-JCPyV antibody index (3.61). After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs. He presented with leukopenia (0.83 × 10^9/L) at hospital admission.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: JC polyomavirus reactivation causing demyelinating brain infection in immunosuppressed patients. This is a leading concern given prior natalizumab exposure, a high anti-JCPyV antibody index, and new focal neurological symptoms; MRI and cerebrospinal fluid JCPyV PCR are needed for evaluation.

PML-associated immune reconstitution inf.description: Inflammatory worsening of underlying PML as immune surveillance recovers after withdrawal of immunosuppressive treatment, including natalizumab. This possibility requires evidence of PML and associated inflammation on imaging.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A syndrome of predominantly posterior cerebral vasogenic edema that can cause seizures and visual disturbances. It is associated with hypertension, endothelial injury, and certain immunomodulatory drugs, and has rarely been reported with fingolimod.

Multiple sclerosis relapse or rebound di.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis relapse or rebound disease activity after natalizumab withdrawal
Multiple sclerosis relapse or rebound di.description: Renewed inflammatory demyelination following natalizumab discontinuation, potentially occurring despite initiation of another disease-modifying treatment.

Herpes simplex encephalitis.description: An acute viral brain infection, usually affecting temporal and frontal regions, that can produce seizures and focal neurological deficits. Immunosuppressive treatment increases concern for serious CNS infections.

case: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

Fabry disease (classic phenotype).description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic GLA variants and deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity, resulting in glycosphingolipid accumulation in nerves, skin, eyes, kidneys, and the cardiovascular system. This patient's markedly reduced enzyme activity and hemizygous GLA c.617T>C (p.Leu206Pro) variant support the diagnosis.

case: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma.description: Secondary bacterial infection of a traumatic liver hematoma, potentially progressing to a hepatic abscess. This is a leading concern with new fever and leukocytosis after several days in the ICU.

Acute acalculous cholecystitis.description: Gallbladder inflammation without gallstones, often associated with critical illness, major trauma, impaired gallbladder emptying, and ischemia.

Infected biloma following traumatic bile.normalized_text: Infected biloma following traumatic bile duct injury
Infected biloma following traumatic bile.description: An infected collection of leaked bile caused by traumatic disruption of intrahepatic bile ducts, which may become apparent days after liver injury.

Acute cholangitis.description: Bacterial infection of the bile ducts, usually associated with impaired biliary drainage. Traumatic duct injury or obstruction by blood clots could predispose to this condition.

Post-traumatic hepatic necrosis.description: Death of liver tissue due to disrupted blood supply after severe hepatic trauma, sometimes complicated by secondary infection.

case: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

Bullous iododerma.description: A rare inflammatory skin reaction to iodine-containing substances, including iodinated contrast, that can cause pustules, vegetating plaques, and hemorrhagic or pus-filled bullae. This is the strongest fit for the exposure and biopsy findings.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: An acute, usually drug-induced eruption characterized by widespread sterile, nonfollicular pustules. Iodinated contrast can be a trigger.

Bullous Sweet syndrome.description: A variant of acute neutrophilic dermatosis that produces inflammatory plaques, vesicles, or bullae with a sterile neutrophilic dermal infiltrate.

Generalized pustular psoriasis.description: A severe inflammatory psoriasis variant causing widespread sterile pustules that may merge into larger collections of pus.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal.description: A severe, usually medication-associated mucocutaneous reaction characterized by extensive keratinocyte death, blistering, and epidermal detachment.

case: 54-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to cardiology clinic for follow-up 20 months since her most recent office visit. She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. The patient was in her usual state of health and asymptomatic without changes in her exercise tolerance, weight, or energy levels. She did not have any gross hematuria or flank pain.

45-year-old man with acute onset nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting starting the day before admission. Three days earlier, he sustained dog bites to both hands and forearms while bathing his dog; he also had recent head trauma from a rusty nail and dental extractions 1–2 weeks prior. Past history includes asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse (up to 18 beers daily, stopped 3 days before admission). On exam he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic, with temperature 35.6°C, blood pressure 154/102 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. He had multiple lacerations with necrotic edges and scratch marks on the hands and forearms, including a 3–4 cm right forearm lesion with a 5–7 cm purplish surrounding border, and capillary refill of 5 seconds.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis followi.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis following dog bites
Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis followi.description: A potentially fulminant bloodstream infection transmitted through dog saliva. Heavy alcohol use increases the risk of severe infection, which may cause shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and purpura. This is a leading concern requiring emergency evaluation.

Dog-bite-associated necrotizing soft tis.description: A rapidly progressive bacterial infection involving deeper soft tissues, potentially caused by mixed organisms introduced through animal bites. Necrosis and systemic illness warrant urgent surgical assessment.

Pasteurella multocida wound infection wi.normalized_text: Pasteurella multocida wound infection with possible bacteremia
Pasteurella multocida wound infection wi.description: An infection caused by bacteria commonly present in dog and cat mouths. Bite wounds may develop cellulitis or deeper infection, with occasional bloodstream spread and sepsis.

Acute alcohol withdrawal syndrome.description: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric symptoms following abrupt reduction or cessation of heavy alcohol consumption. The timing fits withdrawal, which could coexist with a serious wound infection.

Acute alcohol-associated pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation associated with heavy alcohol use, typically producing epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Confirmation requires pancreatic enzyme testing and sometimes imaging.

Tetanus.description: A toxin-mediated infection following contamination of wounds, classically causing jaw stiffness, rigidity, painful spasms, and autonomic instability. Recent injuries provide possible entry sites, but the described presentation lacks characteristic neuromuscular findings.

case: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic.normalized_text: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), associated with an MT-TL1 m.3303C>T variant
Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic.description: The leading diagnosis is a mitochondrial disorder causing impaired energy production, muscle disease, and stroke-like neurological episodes. The reported MT-TL1 variant supports mitochondrial disease; brain imaging is needed to distinguish stroke-like episodes from vascular infarctions.

MT-TL1-related mitochondrial myopathy wi.normalized_text: MT-TL1-related mitochondrial myopathy with cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia and possible cardioembolic stroke
MT-TL1-related mitochondrial myopathy wi.description: MT-TL1-related mitochondrial disease can affect skeletal and cardiac muscle. The m.3303C>T variant has been associated with mitochondrial myopathy and cardiomyopathy; cardiac disease could explain syncope and potentially embolic strokes, although cardiac testing and neuroimaging are required.

Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber.normalized_text: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF) spectrum disorder
Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fiber.description: A mitochondrial encephalomyopathy characterized primarily by myoclonus, epilepsy, ataxia, and mitochondrial myopathy, usually associated with MT-TK variants. It is a less likely mitochondrial differential because the characteristic seizure phenotype is not reported.

Kearns-Sayre syndrome.description: A mitochondrial disorder usually caused by a large mitochondrial DNA deletion, classically featuring onset before age 20, progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction disease. It is less likely because its defining ocular findings are not reported and the identified variant is a point mutation rather than a large deletion.

case: 29-year-old woman with a 7-week history of progressive generalized pruritus, nausea, bloating, and watery mustard-colored diarrhea սկս after eating sushi. Symptoms persisted despite methylprednisolone, hydroxyzine, and diphenoxylate-atropine. Three weeks later, she developed jaundice, right upper quadrant discomfort, decreased appetite, and amber urine. Four weeks before presentation, labs showed elevated ALT 327 U/L, AST 104 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, and CA 19-9 73 U/mL. Past history included anxiety and depression; no medications or drug allergies. On exam, she was thin and jaundiced with scleral icterus and diffuse excoriations.

Acute hepatitis A with cholestatic featu.normalized_text: Acute hepatitis A with cholestatic features
Acute hepatitis A with cholestatic featu.description: A foodborne viral liver infection that can cause prolonged jaundice and intense itching. Exposure usually precedes symptoms by several weeks, so sushi eaten immediately before symptom onset would not explain acquisition.

Acute hepatitis E.description: An enterically transmitted viral hepatitis that can produce gastrointestinal symptoms followed by jaundice, sometimes with prolonged cholestasis.

Clonorchiasis or opisthorchiasis.description: Liver-fluke infection acquired from raw or undercooked freshwater fish. Biliary inflammation or obstruction can cause cholestatic symptoms; the type and origin of the sushi fish are important.

Choledocholithiasis.description: A stone obstructing the common bile duct, causing impaired bile drainage. Benign biliary obstruction can also mildly elevate CA 19-9.

Primary biliary cholangitis.description: An autoimmune disease affecting small intrahepatic bile ducts, predominantly in women, that can cause itching before jaundice. Alkaline phosphatase and antimitochondrial antibody testing help assess this possibility.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis.description: A chronic inflammatory disease causing bile-duct strictures and cholestasis, often associated with inflammatory bowel disease. Biliary imaging is needed to evaluate this diagnosis.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: Immune-mediated liver inflammation that commonly affects young women and may present acutely with jaundice. Autoantibodies, serum IgG, and sometimes liver biopsy support diagnosis.

case: A patient with known Crohn's disease presented with difficulties to pass stool, a sensation of a foreign body in the rectum and limited rectal bleeding. An endoscopy was performed as the first examination. A gallstone was found in the rectum and it was removed without complications.

Rectal gallstone impaction.description: A gallstone lodged in the rectum causes outlet obstruction and local mucosal irritation. Endoscopic identification and uncomplicated removal establish this as the immediate cause of the presentation.

Cholecystoenteric fistula with passage o.normalized_text: Cholecystoenteric fistula with passage of a gallstone into the colon
Cholecystoenteric fistula with passage o.description: An abnormal connection between the gallbladder and intestine can allow a large gallstone to enter the bowel and migrate to the rectum. This is a possible underlying mechanism, but the fistula and its location are not established by the information provided.

Crohn's-related anorectal stricture.description: Chronic Crohn's inflammation can cause anorectal scarring and narrowing, potentially impairing stool passage or contributing to stone impaction. A stricture is not documented in this case.

case: 15-year-old boy presented after injuring his left knee while carrying a tray of food at a fast food restaurant. He felt his knee 'wobble' and fell to the floor, unable to bear weight due to pain. Medical history included chronic fatigue syndrome. Had a Beighton score of 6 (indicating joint laxity) but no history of joint dislocations. On examination: laterally dislocated patella, moderate effusion, pain on palpation around medial patellofemoral ligament, range of movement reduced to extension-flexion of 0/10/60 degrees, ligamentous tests unremarkable. Two weeks later: complained of intermittent locking in left knee, had joint effusion and palpable loose body under patella.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella out of the femoral trochlear groove, often facilitated by joint laxity. This is directly supported by the examination findings.

Osteochondral fracture with an intra-art.normalized_text: Osteochondral fracture with an intra-articular loose body
Osteochondral fracture with an intra-art.description: A fragment of cartilage and underlying bone can detach from the patella or lateral femoral condyle during patellar dislocation, causing persistent swelling and mechanical locking.

Medial patellofemoral ligament tear.description: Injury to the main ligament resisting lateral patellar displacement, commonly occurring during an acute lateral patellar dislocation.

Displaced meniscal tear.description: A torn meniscal fragment, particularly a bucket-handle tear, can displace within the knee and produce mechanical locking after injury.

Unstable juvenile osteochondritis dissec.normalized_text: Unstable juvenile osteochondritis dissecans with loose-body formation
Unstable juvenile osteochondritis dissec.description: A focal disorder of subchondral bone in adolescents that can destabilize the overlying cartilage and release an osteochondral fragment into the joint.

case: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by spiny follicular papules on the trunk and limbs, scarring scalp alopecia, and usually nonscarring axillary and pubic hair loss. This is the strongest diagnostic consideration, although the type of alopecia requires examination and biopsy.

Lichen planopilaris.description: An inflammatory follicular disorder that causes perifollicular redness and scaling, itching, and permanent scarring hair loss. The Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome represents a distinctive presentation within this spectrum.

Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides.description: A form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma involving hair follicles that can produce persistent itchy follicular papules and alopecia. Skin biopsies are needed to distinguish it from inflammatory follicular disorders.

Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalva.description: A rare, often inherited follicular keratinization disorder producing widespread spiny follicular papules and progressive scarring alopecia, usually beginning in childhood.

Pityriasis rubra pilaris.description: A keratinization disorder characterized by follicular keratotic papules, orange-red scaly plaques, and often thickening of the palms and soles.

case: 35-year-old woman with severe hypertension, oedema, and renal failure. She had a pregnancy 12 months earlier complicated by preeclampsia, requiring Caesarean delivery at 29 weeks, followed by persistent poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria >1 g/day. Over the preceding 6 months, she developed fatigue, headaches, worsening hypertension, and facial and pedal oedema. She denied fever, neurologic symptoms, or diarrhoeal prodrome. On examination, she was pale and hydrated with blood pressure 151/103 mmHg. Labs showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked renal dysfunction, proteinuria 4.9 g/24 h with hematuria, elevated LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, schistocytes, increased reticulocytes, and a negative Coombs test; liver enzymes, immunologic tests, viral screening, and antiphospholipid antibodies were normal.

Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.normalized_text: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome)
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.description: Complement dysregulation causes small-vessel endothelial injury, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and predominantly renal organ damage. Pregnancy can trigger the disease. This is the leading consideration, but confirmation requires evaluation for other thrombotic microangiopathies.

Hypertension-associated thrombotic micro.description: Severe hypertension can injure renal arterioles and cause renal failure, microangiopathic hemolysis, and thrombocytopenia. Hypertension can also be a consequence of another thrombotic microangiopathy rather than its primary cause.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.description: Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency causes platelet-rich microvascular thrombi, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. It is an urgent alternative to exclude with ADAMTS13 testing.

Shiga toxin-associated hemolytic uremic.description: Shiga toxin-producing bacterial infection can cause microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, usually following diarrhoeal illness.

HELLP syndrome.description: A pregnancy-associated syndrome of hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, usually occurring late in pregnancy or shortly after delivery. It could resemble the earlier obstetric illness but is very unlikely to explain the current presentation.

case: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Ileal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GI.normalized_text: Ileal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), KIT exon 11–mutant
Ileal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GI.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract, commonly driven by activating KIT mutations. The ileal wall mass and KIT exon 11 deletion strongly support this diagnosis; histopathology and immunohistochemistry provide confirmation.

Ileal neuroendocrine tumor.description: A tumor arising from neuroendocrine cells of the small intestine that can appear as an enhancing ileal mass. It is substantially less likely than GIST given the reported KIT mutation.

Primary ileal leiomyosarcoma.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the intestinal wall that may form an enhancing mass and bleed through mucosal ulceration. Pathology distinguishes it from GIST.

Ileal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the small intestine that can cause bleeding and anemia, although it more often produces irregular wall thickening or an obstructing lesion than a discrete enhancing mural mass.

case: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the stomach that can grow outward into the abdomen, producing a large mass before causing prominent symptoms.

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant pancreatic tumor that may impair digestion and glucose regulation; a sufficiently large tumor can produce abdominal fullness or a palpable mass.

Pancreatic pseudocyst.description: An encapsulated pancreatic fluid collection, usually following pancreatitis, that can compress the stomach and cause upper abdominal fullness.

Intra-abdominal non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that can form bulky abdominal lymph-node masses or involve the gastrointestinal tract.

Mesenteric cyst.description: A usually benign fluid-filled lesion in the intestinal mesentery that can enlarge and cause a painless abdominal mass and pressure-related digestive symptoms.

case: A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

Hailey-Hailey disease (familial benign c.description: An inherited disorder of skin-cell adhesion causing recurrent fragile blisters, painful erosions, and macerated plaques, typically in skin folds. Heat, sweating, and friction worsen the disease. This is the leading consideration.

Darier disease.description: An inherited disorder of epidermal adhesion and keratinization producing persistent, often greasy or crusted papules and plaques. Flexural disease may become macerated and malodorous.

Pemphigus vegetans.description: A rare autoimmune blistering disorder in which blisters and erosions evolve into thickened, vegetating plaques, often in intertriginous areas.

Chronic intertrigo with secondary candid.normalized_text: Chronic intertrigo with secondary candidal or bacterial infection
Chronic intertrigo with secondary candid.description: Inflammation caused by moisture and friction in skin folds, sometimes complicated by fungal or bacterial overgrowth that causes odor, crusting, and erosions.

Inverse psoriasis.description: A form of psoriasis affecting skin folds, where plaques are often smooth and have little scale because of moisture and friction.

case: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst.description: A functional ovarian cyst containing blood that can cause a unilateral pelvic mass and tenderness. Pelvic ultrasound is needed to characterize it.

Ovarian mature cystic teratoma (dermoid.description: A usually benign ovarian germ-cell tumor common in young women that may cause a palpable mass, pressure, or pain.

Ovarian endometrioma.description: An ovarian cyst caused by endometriosis, containing old blood and potentially producing pelvic pain and an adnexal mass.

Adnexal torsion associated with an ovari.normalized_text: Adnexal torsion associated with an ovarian mass
Adnexal torsion associated with an ovari.description: Twisting of the ovary or fallopian tube, often around an existing mass, which can compromise blood supply and requires urgent assessment when suspected.

Pedunculated subserosal uterine leiomyom.description: A benign uterine smooth-muscle tumor growing outward on a stalk that can resemble an ovarian mass and become tender with degeneration or torsion.

case: 36-year-old female with no past medical history who developed lower limbs and para-spinal muscle spasms that progressed over 3 months. Her symptoms continued to progress and she became wheelchair-bound 6 months later. When reviewed at institution, she was severely disabled requiring regular IVIG treatments at a dose of 90g every 12 days. She was taking regular diazepam at a dose of 30mg per day and morphine up to 60mg a day to control pain. On examination, she had brisk reflexes and severe clonus. The muscle spasms were severe enough to compromise her breathing and she required intermittent oxygen.

Stiff-person syndrome.description: An autoimmune disorder of impaired central nervous system inhibition causing progressive axial and limb stiffness with painful spasms. This is the leading diagnostic consideration.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe autoimmune stiff-person spectrum disorder, often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, that produces rigidity, spasms, exaggerated reflexes, and sometimes brainstem or autonomic dysfunction.

Autoimmune inflammatory myelopathy.description: Immune-mediated spinal cord disease that can interrupt descending motor pathways, causing spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and progressive mobility impairment.

Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord invo.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord involvement
Multiple sclerosis with spinal cord invo.description: An inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause spinal cord dysfunction with spasticity, painful spasms, and impaired walking.

Acquired neuromyotonia (Isaacs syndrome).description: A peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder, sometimes autoimmune, causing continuous muscle activity, stiffness, cramps, and impaired relaxation.

case: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.

Cardiac arrhythmia causing syncope.description: An intermittent abnormal heart rhythm can reduce blood flow to the brain and cause sudden collapse. Recurrent unexplained collapse requires prompt assessment for potentially dangerous cardiac causes.

Orthostatic hypotension.description: A fall in blood pressure on standing can cause dizziness, fainting, or collapse. Confirmation requires a positional history and lying and standing blood pressure measurements.

Vasovagal syncope.description: A reflex-mediated decrease in blood pressure, sometimes accompanied by a slow heart rate, causes transient loss of consciousness. Typical triggers and warning symptoms are not described in this case.

Post-stroke epilepsy.description: A previous stroke can leave a brain lesion that predisposes to seizures, which may cause impaired awareness and falls. The likelihood depends on stroke location and details of the collapse episodes.

Carotid sinus syndrome.description: An exaggerated carotid sinus reflex can cause a sudden drop in heart rate or blood pressure and resulting syncope, sometimes triggered by neck movement or pressure. Prior carotid surgery alone does not establish this diagnosis.

case: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and adalimumab. Four months before admission, she developed pain and stiffness in the MCP and IP joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission, she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli. Labs then showed anemia, leukopenia/neutropenia, elevated rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinemia, ANA 1:640, low C4, positive cryoglobulins, and negative HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C serologies. On admission, she had fever and pancytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy; blood film, cultures, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT, peripheral blood CMV PCR, and tuberculin skin test were negative. She had traveled to Athens 7 months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: Systemic infection of macrophages by Leishmania, particularly L. infantum in the Mediterranean. Sand flies transmit infection from reservoirs including dogs; methotrexate and adalimumab increase susceptibility. It can mimic autoimmune disease and cause secondary cryoglobulinemia.

Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: Immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis associated with cryoglobulins, often caused by infection, autoimmune disease, or a lymphoproliferative disorder. Negative hepatitis serologies do not exclude nonviral causes.

Adalimumab-induced lupus-like syndrome.description: An autoimmune syndrome triggered by TNF inhibitors that can cause fever, inflammatory joint symptoms, cutaneous disease, autoantibodies, and occasionally cytopenias or hypocomplementemia.

Felty syndrome.description: A complication of rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia and usually splenomegaly, with increased infection risk and occasional vasculitic manifestations. Splenomegaly is not mandatory.

T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukem.description: A clonal T-cell disorder strongly associated with rheumatoid arthritis, frequently producing neutropenia and anemia. An unrevealing peripheral blood film does not exclude a low-burden disorder.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A severe hyperinflammatory syndrome triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. Visceral leishmaniasis is a possible trigger; ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, and additional diagnostic studies would be needed.

case: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic inflammatory skin disorder associated with diabetes that typically causes slowly enlarging pretibial plaques with central atrophy. This is the leading consideration.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A benign diabetes-associated skin condition causing small, brown, atrophic patches, usually on both shins.

Morphea.description: Localized skin inflammation and fibrosis that can evolve into a hyperpigmented, sclerotic plaque with subsequent atrophy or depression.

Atrophic dermatofibroma.description: A benign fibrous skin lesion, often occurring on the legs of young adults, that can appear brown and depressed and occasionally be tender.

Lupus panniculitis.description: An inflammatory disorder of subcutaneous fat that causes tender plaques or nodules and may heal with depressed scars due to fat loss; systemic lupus need not be present.

case: 14-year-old boy with acute fear of choking and swallowing since 2 days after choking on chicken, followed by vomiting with attempted eating, markedly reduced oral intake, and drooling. Mother reported inspiratory stridor during sleep for several weeks before presentation. On the day of admission he could only take small sips of water and was sleeping most of the day. History includes term birth with nuchal cord and initial resuscitation, infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, sensory-integration training in childhood, incomplete immunizations after age 2.5 years, keratosis pilaris, and eczema. Exam showed an alert, anxious-appearing boy with persistent involuntary burping, dry oral mucosa, drooling, normal cranial nerves, speech, gait, strength, sensation, and reflexes; later exam noted hypertonic leg muscles and mildly positive left Chvostek sign.

Esophageal food bolus impaction or retai.normalized_text: Esophageal food bolus impaction or retained foreign body
Esophageal food bolus impaction or retai.description: An acute esophageal obstruction after eating, potentially associated with underlying esophageal narrowing or inflammation. Drooling and inability to tolerate liquids warrant urgent assessment.

Eosinophilic esophagitis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory disease of the esophagus associated with atopy, dysphagia, and food impaction, particularly in boys and young men.

Choking phobia (phagophobia).description: An anxiety-related fear of swallowing that can follow a choking event and lead to severe food avoidance. Mechanical and neurologic causes must be excluded before attributing this presentation to anxiety.

Hypocalcemic tetany with laryngospasm.description: Low ionized calcium can cause neuromuscular irritability, muscle hypertonia, and potentially dangerous laryngeal spasm. A mildly positive Chvostek sign alone is not diagnostic.

Tetanus.description: A toxin-mediated infection causing muscle rigidity, spasms, and sometimes dysphagia or laryngospasm. Incomplete immunization increases concern, although the absence of reported trismus, characteristic spasms, or a wound makes this presentation less typical.

Achalasia.description: An esophageal motility disorder characterized by impaired lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and absent normal peristalsis, causing dysphagia, regurgitation, and occasionally nocturnal respiratory symptoms.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease with ref.normalized_text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease with reflux-related laryngospasm
Gastroesophageal reflux disease with ref.description: Reflux can cause esophageal irritation, regurgitation, belching, and episodic laryngeal closure, including during sleep. Uncomplicated reflux would not adequately explain severe acute swallowing impairment.

case: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with recurrent fever. Four months earlier, bleeding from a right scalp lesion led to evaluation showing ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months earlier, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which showed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 nodes; BRAF V600E mutation was identified. She started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib 1 month before admission and developed fever and nausea the day after starting therapy, which improved after temporary discontinuation and antipyretics. Fever recurred 2 weeks before admission. On presentation, temperature was 40.2°C, pulse 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 85/53 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air; she was diaphoretic, ill appearing, with mild right upper quadrant tenderness and no rash.

Dabrafenib–trametinib-associated pyrexia.description: A common adverse reaction to combined BRAF and MEK inhibition that can cause recurrent high fever, dehydration, and hypotension. The timing and improvement after treatment interruption make this the leading possibility, although infection must be excluded urgently.

Sepsis from an occult bacterial infectio.normalized_text: Sepsis from an occult bacterial infection
Sepsis from an occult bacterial infectio.description: A potentially life-threatening systemic response to infection. High fever with apparent hypotension requires urgent evaluation for sepsis even when a medication reaction is suspected.

Acute ascending cholangitis.description: An infection of the biliary tract, usually associated with biliary obstruction, that can cause fever, right upper quadrant pain, and hemodynamic instability.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A rare, severe hyperinflammatory syndrome that may be triggered by malignancy, infection, or medications, including rarely BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Diagnosis requires additional evidence such as cytopenias, markedly elevated ferritin, and other inflammatory abnormalities.

Adrenal crisis.description: Acute cortisol deficiency can produce hypotension, fever, nausea, and abdominal discomfort. It is a less supported possibility here because no adrenal disease, glucocorticoid withdrawal, or other clear precipitating history is provided.

case: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. In August 2011, presented to emergency room with abdominal pain. Lab tests showed elevated lipase (874 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (289 IU/L), and ALT (222 IU/L), with normal bilirubin. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase of 357 IU/L and normal serum lipase.

Acute cholecystitis.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by cystic duct obstruction from a gallstone. This is the leading explanation for the later presentation; imaging is needed for confirmation.

Gallstone pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation caused by transient obstruction of the pancreatic outflow by a gallstone. It could explain the initial episode, followed by a separate gallbladder complication.

Choledocholithiasis with intermittent bi.description: A stone in the common bile duct can intermittently obstruct bile flow, elevate liver enzymes, and precipitate pancreatitis.

Gallbladder metastasis from prostate can.normalized_text: Gallbladder metastasis from prostate cancer causing secondary cholecystitis
Gallbladder metastasis from prostate can.description: An exceptionally rare metastatic deposit in the gallbladder could obstruct its drainage or inflame its wall, mimicking ordinary cholecystitis. Confirmation would require imaging and histopathology.

Malignant biliary obstruction related to.normalized_text: Malignant biliary obstruction related to metastatic prostate cancer
Malignant biliary obstruction related to.description: Metastatic tumor or lymphadenopathy involving the biliary region can compress bile ducts, causing cholestasis and sometimes gallbladder distention. The documented periaortic nodes alone do not establish biliary compression.

case: 13-year-old boy with progressive symptoms including Addison’s disease, dysphagia, muscle weakness, severe fatigue, and recent gait ataxia. Born at term with bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and hypospadias. Early development was initially normal, but later global developmental delay and mild intellectual disability were noted by age 9. He had absent tear production since infancy. At age 2, he developed recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, and progressive hyperpigmentation; at age 4, recurrent hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia led to diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Progressive dysphagia began at age 11 and later required liquids to swallow. Examination showed severe hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles, facial dysmorphism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal arm weakness and wasting, milder pyramidal weakness in the legs, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin, consistent with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency.

Allgrove syndrome (triple-A syndrome), w.normalized_text: Allgrove syndrome (triple-A syndrome), with neurologic involvement
Allgrove syndrome (triple-A syndrome), w.description: An autosomal recessive disorder, usually caused by AAAS variants, characterized by alacrima, esophageal achalasia, and ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency. Progressive neurologic and autonomic dysfunction may occur. This is the strongest unifying diagnosis; achalasia requires confirmation.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.description: An ABCD1-related disorder of very-long-chain fatty acid metabolism that can cause primary adrenal insufficiency and progressive cerebral or spinal neurologic disease in boys.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency.description: A group of inherited disorders causing selective cortisol deficiency, often through impaired ACTH signaling, with markedly elevated ACTH and generally preserved mineralocorticoid function.

Congenital alacrima-achalasia-intellectu.description: A rare GMPPA-related autosomal recessive disorder causing congenital alacrima, achalasia, and developmental impairment. Unlike Allgrove syndrome, adrenal insufficiency is generally absent.

Familial dysautonomia.description: An ELP1-related hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy causing impaired tear production, swallowing and gastrointestinal dysfunction, temperature instability, and progressive neurologic impairment.

case: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, stage IV with metastases to bone, lungs, and liver, status post mastectomy, multiple systemic therapies, and stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier. Most recent treatment was anastrozole for 3 months and paracetamol for pain. She developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion over several days, rapidly worsening to unresponsiveness. On admission, she was found on the floor, disoriented, with lower leg weakness and inability to follow basic instructions. Exam showed an awake but unresponsive, uncooperative patient without initial focal neurologic deficits; vital signs were afebrile with normal blood pressure and mild tachycardia. Baseline brain MRI 2 weeks earlier was normal.

Hepatic encephalopathy due to extensive.normalized_text: Hepatic encephalopathy due to extensive liver metastases
Hepatic encephalopathy due to extensive.description: Impaired liver function from metastatic infiltration can cause accumulation of neurotoxins and progressive encephalopathy, potentially leading to coma.

Hypercalcemia of malignancy.description: Cancer-associated elevation of serum calcium, particularly with extensive bone metastases, can cause muscular weakness, confusion, and coma.

Leptomeningeal metastasis from breast ca.description: Dissemination of breast cancer cells into the leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid can produce multifocal neurologic dysfunction and altered consciousness. Early disease may not be visible on MRI.

Nonconvulsive status epilepticus.description: Persistent or recurrent seizures without prominent convulsions can cause an awake but unresponsive state, confusion, and inability to follow commands.

Hypoglycemic encephalopathy.description: Severe glucose depletion can impair brain function and cause weakness, behavioral changes, seizures, or coma; advanced liver involvement may increase susceptibility.

Hyponatremic encephalopathy.description: A substantial or rapid decrease in serum sodium can cause cerebral edema, resulting in confusion, weakness, seizures, and reduced consciousness.

Brain metastases with cerebral edema.description: Intracranial spread of breast cancer can cause neurologic deficits, seizures, or altered consciousness through direct tissue involvement and surrounding edema.

case: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history developed progressive weakness in all four extremities and sensory changes over 1 month, followed by urinary difficulty. Examination showed hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski sign, bilateral Hoffmann and Tromner signs, and asymmetric motor weakness (MRC 2/5 on the right, 4/5 on the left). Sensory loss included decreased pinprick and temperature sensation below C4, more on the left, and decreased vibration and proprioception, more on the right. Serologic autoimmune studies and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal; angiotensin-converting enzyme was mildly elevated. Brain MRI, chest and abdominal CT, and nerve conduction study showed no other organ involvement.

Compressive cervical myelopathy.description: Cervical spinal cord compression from degenerative disease, disc herniation, or a mass can cause progressive weakness, sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction. Cervical spine MRI is needed to identify or exclude compression.

Spinal neurosarcoidosis.description: Granulomatous inflammation involving the spinal cord can produce subacute cervical myelopathy, occasionally without detectable systemic sarcoidosis. Mild serum angiotensin-converting enzyme elevation is nonspecific and does not establish this diagnosis.

Inflammatory transverse myelitis.description: Inflammation of the spinal cord, either idiopathic or associated with an immune-mediated disorder, can cause motor, sensory, and autonomic deficits. Spinal MRI and targeted antibody testing help distinguish its causes.

Cervical intramedullary ependymoma.description: An ependymoma is a spinal cord tumor seen in adults that can cause progressive cervical myelopathy through cord expansion and disruption of motor and sensory pathways.

Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula causi.normalized_text: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula causing cervical venous congestive myelopathy
Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula causi.description: An abnormal arteriovenous connection can impair spinal venous drainage and produce progressive cord dysfunction. Cervical cord involvement is uncommon but can cause quadriparesis; MRI and vascular imaging are needed for evaluation.

case: 33-year-old male with 20 days of cough and small amounts of yellow-white sticky sputum սկս after a cold. No hemoptysis, fever, chills, dyspnea, or initial chest pain. Treated at a local clinic with intravenous therapy without improvement. Cough worsened 7 days before admission, especially at night causing sleep disturbance, sometimes with right-sided chest pain. Past history unremarkable; smokes about 10 cigarettes/day for >10 years, no alcohol use. Exam: T 36.2℃, P 112/min, R 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg; symmetric chest, equal respiratory movement and vocal fremitus, clear bilateral percussion, coarse breath sounds bilaterally with a small amount of wet rales in the right lung, no dry rales or pleural friction rub.

Acute bronchitis.description: Inflammation of the large airways, usually following a viral respiratory infection, with cough that can persist for several weeks. Sputum color alone does not establish a bacterial cause.

Community-acquired pneumonia.description: Infection of the lung tissue that may present with cough, sputum, focal crackles, and chest pain. Chest imaging is needed to distinguish it from bronchitis in this case.

Postinfectious cough.description: Persistent cough caused by residual airway inflammation and heightened cough sensitivity after a respiratory infection, typically lasting three to eight weeks. The current duration is near the lower boundary.

Pertussis.description: A bacterial respiratory infection that can cause a prolonged cough after an initially cold-like illness. Adults may lack the classic inspiratory whoop.

Cough-variant asthma.description: An asthma phenotype in which cough is the predominant symptom, often worse at night and triggered by respiratory infections. Confirmation requires assessment for variable airflow limitation or airway hyperresponsiveness.

case: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.normalized_text: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.description: A mosquito-transmitted parasitic infection associated with canine reservoirs and endemic in Mediterranean regions, including Croatia. Humans may develop migrating subcutaneous worms or solitary nodules. Confirmation typically requires excision and identification of the parasite.

Subcutaneous sparganosis.description: Infection by larval Spirometra tapeworms, usually acquired through contaminated water or ingestion of infected animal tissues, that can cause slowly migrating subcutaneous nodules.

Cutaneous gnathostomiasis.description: A tissue-invasive helminth infection, generally acquired from raw or undercooked infected freshwater animals, that produces recurrent migratory subcutaneous swellings.

Lipoma.description: A benign tumor of mature fat that commonly presents as a slow-growing, painless, mobile subcutaneous lump.

Epidermoid cyst.description: A benign keratin-filled cutaneous or subcutaneous cyst that can present as a firm, well-circumscribed painless nodule when not inflamed.

case: 66-year-old man with progressive neurologic symptoms beginning around 2000, including unexplained falls while riding a motorcycle. By October 2003, he developed blurred vision, photophobia, and worsening imbalance/unsteadiness while walking. He had bilateral cataracts and presbyopia treated with bilateral lens implantation in 2000 without benefit. Examination showed irregular pupils with sluggish direct light reflexes, slow and limited vertical gaze, slow horizontal pursuit with bilateral adduction paresis, normal convergence, impaired rapid alternating movements, and a tendency to fall backward. Over time, he developed frequent falls requiring a cane, retrocollis, slurred speech, inability to look down, and dysphagia. By March 2007, he was admitted for dysphagia with repeated aspiration; exam showed fixed up- and outward-deviated eyes with absent vertical and medial eye movements, no convergence, no Bell’s phenomenon, no optokinetic or caloric nystagmus, absent doll’s eye responses, severe nuchal rigidity, inability to sit independently, backward falls, axial rigidity, symmetric minimally brisk reflexes, flexor plantar responses, and no resting tremor.

Progressive supranuclear palsy, Richards.description: A progressive neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by early backward falls, vertical gaze palsy, axial rigidity, and bulbar dysfunction. This is the strongest fit; advanced disease can progress beyond a purely supranuclear eye movement disorder.

Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3.description: An inherited progressive neurodegenerative disorder that can cause gait ataxia, slow eye movements, external ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and rigidity.

Multiple system atrophy.description: A progressive synucleinopathy combining autonomic failure with parkinsonism, cerebellar dysfunction, or both. It can cause rapid deterioration in gait, speech, and swallowing.

Corticobasal degeneration presenting as.normalized_text: Corticobasal degeneration presenting as a progressive supranuclear palsy syndrome
Corticobasal degeneration presenting as.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy usually associated with asymmetric rigidity, limb apraxia, and cortical dysfunction, but occasionally presenting with a progressive supranuclear palsy-like syndrome.

Central nervous system Whipple disease.description: A rare, potentially treatable infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that can involve the brain and mimic progressive supranuclear palsy, sometimes without gastrointestinal manifestations.

case: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

Cryptococcal meningitis.description: An opportunistic fungal infection of the meninges, most commonly caused by Cryptococcus neoformans. This is the leading consideration given advanced HIV, subacute symptoms, and elevated intracranial pressure.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A subacute infection of the meninges caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, with increased risk in advanced HIV.

Cytomegalovirus meningoencephalitis.description: An opportunistic viral infection of the brain and meninges, usually occurring in people with HIV and CD4+ counts below 50 cells/µL.

Herpes simplex virus type 2 meningitis.description: A viral infection of the meninges that can accompany newly acquired or recurrent HSV-2 infection and may be more severe in immunocompromised patients.

Early neurosyphilis presenting as syphil.normalized_text: Early neurosyphilis presenting as syphilitic meningitis
Early neurosyphilis presenting as syphil.description: Central nervous system infection by Treponema pallidum that can cause meningitis during early syphilis; HIV coinfection increases clinical concern.

case: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

Acute brainstem ischemic stroke causing.normalized_text: Acute brainstem ischemic stroke causing left internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Acute brainstem ischemic stroke causing.description: The leading diagnosis is a small infarction affecting the left medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons or midbrain. Sudden onset and atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation strongly support ischemia; urgent stroke assessment is warranted.

Demyelinating disease causing internucle.description: Demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis, can disrupt coordinated horizontal eye movements. A first presentation at age 83 is highly unusual.

Ocular myasthenia gravis with pseudo-int.normalized_text: Ocular myasthenia gravis with pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Ocular myasthenia gravis with pseudo-int.description: Autoimmune dysfunction of neuromuscular transmission can cause variable extraocular muscle weakness and occasionally mimic internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

Partial left oculomotor nerve palsy.description: A partial third cranial nerve palsy can weaken the left medial rectus muscle and impair adduction, although the paired finding of contralateral abducting nystagmus favors internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

Right-eye optical monocular diplopia.description: An optical abnormality such as cataract, irregular astigmatism, or tear-film disturbance can cause double vision that persists when the affected eye views alone. It would not explain the neurological eye-movement findings and could only be a concurrent condition or reflect ambiguity in the history.

case: 35-day-old male infant, born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation, previously healthy and fed breast milk plus formula, presented with 2 days of worsening fussiness, pallor, fever, vomiting, mottled skin, and respiratory distress. The day before admission he was noted to be pale and warm with one episode of vomiting; on admission he had tachycardia and increased vomiting. Exam showed temperature 39.1°C, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, oxygen saturation 97% on 1 L nasal cannula, pallor, listlessness, mottled cool extremities, a grade 2/6 holosystolic-flow murmur, and splenomegaly 2–3 cm below the costal margin. Urinalysis showed dark red cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts.

Neonatal babesiosis.description: A parasitic infection of red blood cells that can rarely be transmitted congenitally and present weeks after birth. Severe disease causes hemolytic anemia and organ dysfunction; confirmation requires blood smear or PCR.

Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis, po.normalized_text: Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis, potentially from a urinary source
Late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis, po.description: An invasive bacterial infection in a young infant that can rapidly cause shock, respiratory distress, and kidney injury. This presentation requires immediate emergency evaluation and treatment.

Congenital malaria.description: A maternally transmitted Plasmodium infection that may become symptomatic several weeks after birth, producing fever, hemolytic anemia, and splenomegaly. Likelihood depends strongly on maternal residence or travel in a malaria-endemic region.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase defici.normalized_text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency with acute hemolysis
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase defici.description: An inherited red-cell enzyme deficiency, most often clinically apparent in males, that can cause acute hemolysis during infection or after oxidant exposure.

Hereditary spherocytosis with an infecti.normalized_text: Hereditary spherocytosis with an infection-associated hemolytic crisis
Hereditary spherocytosis with an infecti.description: An inherited red-cell membrane disorder causing splenic destruction of red blood cells and anemia, which can worsen during infection and occasionally present in early infancy.

case: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

Recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with p.normalized_text: Recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with pelvic or rectal involvement
Recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with p.description: High-grade prostate cancer can recur years after prostatectomy and invade or compress nearby pelvic structures, including the rectum. The prior Gleason 9 tumor makes recurrence an important concern requiring prompt evaluation.

Primary rectal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of the rectal lining that can cause a persistent urge to defecate, rectal discomfort, and systemic symptoms, particularly in advanced disease.

Anal squamous cell carcinoma.description: A malignancy of the anal canal that may cause persistent anorectal pain and, when locally advanced, obstructive symptoms and weight loss.

Rectal or pelvic lymphoma.description: A malignancy of lymphoid tissue that can rarely involve the rectum or form a pelvic mass, producing local pressure symptoms and systemic illness.

Deep anorectal abscess.description: An infection forming a collection of pus around the rectum or anus; a deep abscess may cause persistent rectal pain and pressure without obvious external swelling.

case: 27-year-old man with 3 days of upper leg myalgias followed by acute worsening weakness on presentation, unable to lift legs or stand, with associated arm weakness. For several months he had insomnia, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremor. He started an herbal stress supplement 4 days before presentation. Exam showed bilateral conjunctival injection, proximal weakness (4/5 upper extremities, 3/5 lower extremities), brisk patellar reflexes, and fine hand tremor. Labs revealed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L), mild transaminitis, elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, elevated CK and aldolase, and venous pH 7.29.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, potential.normalized_text: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, potentially due to Graves disease
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, potential.description: The leading possibility: excess thyroid hormone promotes potassium movement into cells, causing profound hypokalemia and acute weakness, especially in young men. Thyroid testing is needed for confirmation. Potassium of 1.8 mmol/L with paralysis requires emergency cardiac monitoring and treatment.

Supplement-associated hypokalemic paraly.description: An herbal product could cause potassium depletion or redistribution through laxative, stimulant, thyroid-active, or other ingredients. The temporal association warrants ingredient review but does not establish causation.

Familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle ion-channel disorder causing episodic weakness from potassium redistribution into cells. A first recognized attack can occur in a young adult, although secondary causes must be excluded.

Renal tubular acidosis causing hypokalem.normalized_text: Renal tubular acidosis causing hypokalemic paralysis
Renal tubular acidosis causing hypokalem.description: A renal acid-handling disorder, particularly distal renal tubular acidosis, can produce metabolic acidosis and substantial urinary potassium loss, resulting in paralysis. Confirmation requires bicarbonate, anion gap, and urine studies.

Thyrotoxic myopathy.description: Excess thyroid hormone can cause proximal muscle weakness and wasting, usually developing gradually. It could coexist with hypokalemic periodic paralysis but would not adequately explain the abrupt episode alone.

case: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.

Congenital double lip.description: A congenital fold of excess tissue on the inner lip that may trap food and interfere with oral hygiene. This is a possibility if the mass involves the lip; its location was not provided.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign bony prominence along the midline of the hard palate, usually requiring no treatment unless it interferes with oral function or hygiene.

Oral hamartoma.description: A benign developmental overgrowth of tissues normally found in the mouth, potentially involving the tongue or adjacent structures.

Oral lymphatic malformation.description: A congenital malformation of lymphatic vessels that can produce a painless oral swelling, commonly involving the tongue.

case: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar disc herniation with left-sided r.normalized_text: Lumbar disc herniation with left-sided radiculopathy
Lumbar disc herniation with left-sided r.description: A herniated lumbar disc compresses a nerve root, causing radiating leg pain and potentially focal weakness. This is the most likely explanation; new weakness of approximately 3/5 warrants urgent assessment and lumbar MRI.

Degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis.description: Degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal or neural foramina can compress lumbar nerves, causing back pain, radiating leg pain, and weakness.

Lumbar spondylolisthesis with nerve-root.description: Slippage of one lumbar vertebra relative to another can produce mechanical back pain and narrow the spaces through which nerve roots pass.

Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst causing.normalized_text: Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst causing radiculopathy
Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst causing.description: A cyst arising from a degenerative lumbar facet joint can compress an adjacent nerve root. Enlargement or bleeding into the cyst can occasionally cause sudden symptoms.

case: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome wi.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome with neurologic and cardiac involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome wi.description: A leading consideration characterized by marked, otherwise unexplained eosinophilia with eosinophil-mediated organ injury. Neurologic dysfunction can result from cerebral thrombosis, embolism, or direct tissue injury. Confirmation requires further exclusion of secondary and clonal causes.

Eosinophilic myocarditis or endomyocardi.normalized_text: Eosinophilic myocarditis or endomyocarditis with cardioembolic cerebral ischemia
Eosinophilic myocarditis or endomyocardi.description: Eosinophilic cardiac inflammation can cause myocardial injury and endocardial thrombosis, potentially producing cerebral emboli. This could explain the combined cardiac and neurologic findings, although brain imaging, further cardiac imaging, and possibly biopsy are needed.

Clonal hypereosinophilia due to a myeloi.normalized_text: Clonal hypereosinophilia due to a myeloid neoplasm
Clonal hypereosinophilia due to a myeloi.description: A hematologic disorder, such as chronic eosinophilic leukemia or a myeloid neoplasm with an eosinophilia-associated kinase fusion, can cause persistent eosinophilia and cardiac or neurologic organ injury. A normal basic neoplasm evaluation does not exclude these disorders; molecular and bone marrow testing may be necessary.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: An eosinophilic small- and medium-vessel vasculitis, formerly called Churg-Strauss syndrome, usually associated with asthma and sinonasal disease. It may affect the heart and nervous system, but this presentation lacks several characteristic features.

Tissue-invasive helminth infection with.normalized_text: Tissue-invasive helminth infection with secondary hypereosinophilia
Tissue-invasive helminth infection with.description: Certain parasitic infections can cause profound eosinophilia and, less commonly, cardiac or central nervous system injury. This is a lower-probability alternative because the initial assessment found no parasitic cause; its relevance depends on exposure history and targeted testing.

case: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas. It can produce FDG-avid lesions that resemble cancer recurrence; biopsy and exclusion of infectious causes are needed for confirmation.

Malignancy-associated sarcoid-like react.description: A noncaseating granulomatous reaction associated with cancer or its treatment, without necessarily meeting criteria for systemic sarcoidosis. It can mimic metastatic disease on FDG-PET.

Recurrent or metastatic breast cancer.description: Return or distant spread of previously treated breast cancer. Her prior node-positive, stage IIIA disease makes recurrence an important possibility, but FDG uptake alone cannot establish it.

Lymphoma.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that commonly produces FDG-avid disease and can cause cytopenias through marrow or splenic involvement.

Tuberculosis.description: An infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can produce granulomatous, FDG-avid lesions resembling sarcoidosis or malignancy. Negative immune-based tests reduce suspicion but do not completely exclude active infection.

case: 78-year-old woman with 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue, referred for anemia with elevated ESR. Past history: hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination was normal, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status 1. Blood tests showed anemia (Hb 99 g/L), elevated ESR (120 mm/h), mildly raised creatinine and calcium, and mildly increased LDH. Further studies revealed IgG kappa paraprotein, elevated β₂-microglobulin, markedly increased free kappa light chains with high kappa/lambda ratio, and urinary kappa Bence-Jones protein; 24-hour urine protein was normal.

Multiple myeloma, IgG kappa type.description: A malignancy of clonal plasma cells producing monoclonal immunoglobulin and/or light chains. This is the leading consideration, although confirmation requires bone marrow assessment and evaluation of myeloma-defining findings.

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic clonal plasma-cell disorder with a substantial monoclonal protein level or marrow plasma-cell burden but no myeloma-defining events. It remains possible only if the anemia and biochemical abnormalities are unrelated and the free light-chain findings do not meet a myeloma-defining threshold.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A clonal plasma-cell condition with a limited monoclonal protein and marrow plasma-cell burden, without attributable organ damage. The current findings are more concerning for myeloma, but this remains a consideration if the anemia and other abnormalities have separate causes.

Systemic AL amyloidosis associated with.normalized_text: Systemic AL amyloidosis associated with a plasma-cell clone
Systemic AL amyloidosis associated with.description: A disorder in which monoclonal light chains deposit as amyloid in tissues, potentially damaging the kidneys, heart, nerves, and other organs. Kappa-associated disease is possible, although lambda light chains are more common.

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgG kapp.normalized_text: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgG kappa secretion
