Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgG kapp.description: An indolent B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation that usually produces IgM but rarely secretes IgG. Bone marrow morphology and immunophenotyping help distinguish it from a plasma-cell neoplasm.

case: 20-year-old male with 3-year history of bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. Over the past 4 years, he had polydipsia, increased fluid intake, and urinary frequency, recently improved. He also reported blurred vision corrected with glasses, occasional post-exertion headaches, decreased facial hair growth, and occasional morning erections, with no sexual activity history. Past history included generalized nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures and focal right leg seizures from ages 6–13, treated with carbamazepine until age 14. Recent constipation and chronic pilonidal cyst were noted. On examination, he appeared young with minimal facial hair, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, BMI 26.5, bilateral breast enlargement without nipple retraction, masses, or discharge, small testicles (~2.5 cm), a small posterior anal fissure, and a small coccygeal lump with central punctum.

Klinefelter syndrome.description: A sex-chromosome disorder, usually 47,XXY, causing primary testicular failure, small testes, reduced testosterone production, and gynecomastia.

Prolactinoma with secondary hypogonadism.description: A prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor that can suppress gonadal function and, if large, cause headaches or visual field abnormalities. Absence of nipple discharge does not exclude it.

Suprasellar germinoma.description: An intracranial germ-cell tumor occurring predominantly in young people that can involve the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk, causing central diabetes insipidus and pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Craniopharyngioma with hypothalamic-pitu.description: A tumor near the pituitary and hypothalamus that can cause gonadotropin deficiency, other pituitary hormone deficits, visual abnormalities, and occasionally central diabetes insipidus.

Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.description: Deficient hypothalamic or pituitary stimulation of the testes, resulting in incomplete puberty, low testosterone, and small testes; it may occur with or without impaired smell.

Persistent pubertal gynecomastia.description: Benign adolescent breast tissue enlargement caused by a transient imbalance between estrogen and androgen effects that sometimes persists into adulthood.

case: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic anemia and leukocytosis, with blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

MRSA infective endocarditis, likely invo.normalized_text: MRSA infective endocarditis, likely involving the aortic valve
MRSA infective endocarditis, likely invo.description: Infection of the endocardial surface by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, likely affecting the aortic valve and causing aortic regurgitation with systemic septic embolization. This is the most likely unifying diagnosis.

Septic cerebral embolism with ischemic s.normalized_text: Septic cerebral embolism with ischemic stroke
Septic cerebral embolism with ischemic s.description: An infected embolus, most plausibly from left-sided infective endocarditis, can obstruct a cerebral artery and cause stroke. This would be a complication of the underlying infection rather than a separate explanation for all findings.

Hematogenous brain abscess.description: A localized intracerebral infection that can develop when bacteria spread through the bloodstream, including from infective endocarditis or another deep MRSA focus.

Acute bacterial meningitis due to Staphy.normalized_text: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Staphylococcus aureus
Acute bacterial meningitis due to Staphy.description: Infection of the meninges, potentially occurring through bloodstream spread of MRSA. It could complicate bacteremia, although it is less unifying than endocarditis with cerebral embolization.

Atrial fibrillation-associated cardioemb.description: A cerebral artery occlusion caused by a cardiac thrombus associated with atrial fibrillation. This could explain the neurological deficit but would not explain the strong evidence of systemic infection.

case: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.description: The strongly favored diagnosis: an autosomal recessive deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) causing glycogen accumulation, particularly in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Markedly deficient GAA activity and two GAA variants in trans support Pompe disease; elevated pro-BNP raises concern for early cardiac involvement, requiring echocardiographic assessment. Absence of p.D645E does not establish CRIM status.

Late-onset Pompe disease detected by new.normalized_text: Late-onset Pompe disease detected by newborn screening
Late-onset Pompe disease detected by new.description: A GAA-deficiency phenotype in which skeletal and respiratory muscle weakness develops later, usually without prominent infantile cardiomyopathy. Presymptomatic newborn screening can identify affected infants, although this patient's cardiac biomarker elevation favors the infantile phenotype.

GAA pseudodeficiency.description: A benign genetic state producing low GAA activity in laboratory assays without clinically significant glycogen storage. It can cause false-positive Pompe newborn screens but is strongly disfavored here by the confirmatory findings, variants in trans, and biochemical evidence of tissue involvement.

case: 6-year-old girl with a 1-year history of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain after a left-hand fall, including rib pain, right knee pain with limping, and left flank pain radiating to the left leg. Six days before admission she developed back pain, worsening limp, and intermittent fever to 39.8°C; the day before admission she developed periorbital swelling, abdominal distention, and periumbilical discoloration. On examination she was febrile, had bilateral periorbital discoloration, a soft nontender abdomen, slight limping, and pain with external rotation of the right hip. Past history included infantile gastroesophageal reflux and pollen allergy with allergic rhinitis.

Metastatic neuroblastoma.description: A childhood tumor of sympathetic nervous tissue, often arising in the adrenal gland or abdomen. Spread to bone and the orbits can cause skeletal pain, limping, and periorbital bruising.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia.description: A malignancy of immature lymphoid cells that commonly affects children and can produce bone pain, fever, bruising, and abdominal enlargement from organ infiltration.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma with abdominal and.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma with abdominal and skeletal involvement
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma with abdominal and.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that can involve abdominal organs, bone marrow, bones, and occasionally orbital tissues.

Multifocal Langerhans cell histiocytosis.description: A clonal disorder of dendritic cells that can produce destructive bone lesions, particularly in the skull, ribs, spine, and long bones, with systemic involvement in some children.

Chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis.description: An autoinflammatory bone disorder, sometimes called chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, causing recurrent pain at multiple skeletal sites in children.

case: 54-year-old woman without comorbidities presented to emergency department with 12-hour history of redness and painful swelling in left gluteal region. Denied trauma. At admission: afebrile (36.2°C), normal blood pressure (109/65 mmHg), heart rate 89 bpm, mild peripheral oxygen desaturation (92% on room air) without respiratory distress. Rest of physical exam normal.

Gluteal cellulitis.description: A bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue causing diffuse inflammation. Fever may be absent early or in localized disease.

Gluteal cutaneous abscess.description: A localized collection of pus beneath the skin, typically producing painful swelling and surrounding redness. Examination or ultrasound is needed to distinguish it from cellulitis.

Early necrotizing soft tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive infection of deeper soft tissues that requires urgent surgical assessment when suspected. Early findings can resemble cellulitis, and fever or hemodynamic instability may initially be absent.

Inflamed or infected epidermoid cyst.description: Inflammation or infection of a keratin-filled skin cyst can cause sudden localized redness, tenderness, and swelling, sometimes without a previously recognized lump.

Spontaneous gluteal hematoma.description: Bleeding into gluteal soft tissue can produce acute painful swelling and skin discoloration. It is less likely without trauma, anticoagulant exposure, or a bleeding disorder.

case: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Only current medication is daily oral acyclovir. Vital signs normal. Physical exam showed impaired ability to dorsiflex wrists while bringing palms together ('prayer sign'). Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease with s.normalized_text: Chronic graft-versus-host disease with sclerotic skin and fascial involvement
Chronic graft-versus-host disease with s.description: A late complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Sclerotic skin and fascial disease can restrict joint movement; muscle and liver involvement may also occur. This is the leading consideration.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory muscle disease associated with characteristic photosensitive skin eruptions and usually symmetric proximal muscle weakness. Rare cases develop after allogeneic transplantation.

Systemic lupus erythematosus.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can produce photosensitive rash, fever, musculoskeletal symptoms and antinuclear antibodies.

Systemic sclerosis.description: An autoimmune fibrosing disease affecting the skin, blood vessels and sometimes internal organs. Skin tightening and joint contractures may limit hand and wrist mobility.

Eosinophilic fasciitis.description: An inflammatory fibrosing disorder of the fascia that causes limb induration and joint contractures. An eosinophilic fasciitis-like syndrome can occur as part of chronic graft-versus-host disease.

case: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

Acquired perforating dermatosis.description: A strongly associated complication of advanced kidney disease and dialysis in which dermal material is eliminated through the epidermis, producing intensely itchy papules, often with central keratotic plugs.

Prurigo nodularis.description: A chronic inflammatory skin disorder driven by an itch-scratch cycle, causing intensely pruritic, firm papules and nodules. Chronic kidney disease can contribute to its development.

Chronic kidney disease-associated prurit.normalized_text: Chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus with secondary scratch lesions
Chronic kidney disease-associated prurit.description: Persistent itching associated with advanced kidney disease, particularly in dialysis patients. Primary skin lesions are usually absent, but scratching can produce excoriations and papules.

Drug-induced photosensitive dermatitis.description: A phototoxic or photoallergic reaction to medication that causes inflammation and itching on light-exposed skin. Medication timing and examination are necessary to assess this possibility.

Dialysis-associated pseudoporphyria.description: A porphyria-like photodistributed skin disorder associated with dialysis or certain medications, typically producing skin fragility, vesicles, and blisters despite normal porphyrin studies.

case: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst. Initially presented with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later developed acute lower back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission: mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, afebrile, no meningism, GCS 15, and leukocytosis with neutrophilia. By day 2 she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffmann signs. CSF examination and electromyography were normal.

Acute transverse myelitis.description: Inflammation of the spinal cord causing motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction. An asymmetric cervical or upper thoracic lesion could explain this presentation; normal CSF does not exclude it.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.description: An autoimmune disorder that can cause extensive inflammatory spinal cord lesions and optic neuritis. A first attack may present as myelitis alone; spinal MRI and aquaporin-4 antibody testing help establish the diagnosis.

Spinal cord infarction.description: Interruption of spinal cord blood supply causing acute pain, weakness, sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction. It is uncommon in adolescents but can occur with vascular abnormalities or fibrocartilaginous embolism.

Spinal epidural abscess with cord compre.normalized_text: Spinal epidural abscess with cord compression
Spinal epidural abscess with cord compre.description: An infection in the spinal epidural space that can compress the cord and cause rapidly progressive neurological deficits. Fever may be absent; this is an urgent diagnosis to exclude with spinal MRI.

Intramedullary spinal cord tumor with ac.normalized_text: Intramedullary spinal cord tumor with acute edema or hemorrhage
Intramedullary spinal cord tumor with ac.description: A tumor within the spinal cord, such as an astrocytoma or ependymoma, can produce painful asymmetric myelopathy. Associated hemorrhage or edema can cause sudden deterioration.

case: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-A.description: An aggressive leukemia of T-lineage precursors. The patient's age, blast predominance, thrombocytopenia, and T-cell markers favor this diagnosis, although absent TdT is unusual and requires confirmatory evaluation.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: An aggressive mature T-cell leukemia usually affecting older adults. It commonly expresses CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7 while lacking precursor markers; confirmation requires characteristic morphology and supporting genetic findings.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, acute su.description: An aggressive mature T-cell malignancy associated with HTLV-1 infection. Diagnosis requires HTLV-1 testing and compatible morphology and immunophenotyping, typically including CD4 and CD25.

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.normalized_text: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, with leukemic involvement
Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.description: A mature T-cell lymphoma that can rarely involve peripheral blood extensively. This is a lower-probability alternative requiring tissue or marrow assessment and exclusion of defined T-cell neoplasms.

case: A 36-year-old Chinese man presented with a 1-month history of persistent fever. He was previously healthy with no significant past medical history, specifically no prior TB infections, chronic illnesses, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, or immune diseases. He was not taking any regular prescription medications and had not travelled abroad. On admission, vital signs showed temperature 37.2°C, heart rate 119 beats/min, blood pressure 90/48 mmHg, respiration rate 38 breaths/min with oxygen saturation 88%. Physical examination revealed an acutely ill appearance and pulmonary rales in both lungs. He presented with persistent fever, pancytopenia, and hyperferritinemia with clinical deterioration including acute respiratory failure.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome, often triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. Persistent fever, pancytopenia, and hyperferritinemia strongly suggest HLH, but additional diagnostic criteria are required for confirmation.

Disseminated tuberculosis with possible.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with possible secondary HLH
Disseminated tuberculosis with possible.description: Systemic Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the lungs and bone marrow, causing prolonged fever and cytopenias. It can also trigger HLH, even without a previous tuberculosis diagnosis.

Epstein–Barr virus infection with second.normalized_text: Epstein–Barr virus infection with secondary HLH
Epstein–Barr virus infection with second.description: Epstein–Barr virus can provoke severe immune activation and HLH in previously healthy adults, producing fever, cytopenias, elevated ferritin, and multiorgan dysfunction.

Occult lymphoma with secondary HLH.description: An unrecognized lymphoma, particularly a T-cell or natural killer-cell lymphoma, can trigger HLH. Lack of a prior malignancy diagnosis does not exclude this possibility.

Sepsis from severe pulmonary infection,.normalized_text: Sepsis from severe pulmonary infection, with possible secondary HLH
Sepsis from severe pulmonary infection,.description: A severe infection can cause systemic inflammation, hypotension, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Concurrent HLH should be considered when pancytopenia and hyperferritinemia are prominent.

case: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.

Zika virus meningoencephalitis.description: A rare neurological complication of mosquito-borne Zika virus infection. Recent travel in the Pacific, transient rash, and acute febrile encephalitis make this an important consideration, although laboratory confirmation is necessary.

Japanese encephalitis.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis that can cause severe neurological disease, particularly in susceptible travelers. Plausibility depends on the precise locations visited and local transmission.

West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease.description: A mosquito-borne infection that can cause encephalitis and motor weakness, with older adults at increased risk of severe disease. The reported itinerary provides less epidemiological support than for some other arboviruses.

Dengue-associated encephalitis.description: An uncommon neurological manifestation of dengue virus infection, which is transmitted by mosquitoes in many Pacific island settings.

Herpes simplex virus encephalitis.description: An acute, potentially fatal viral infection of brain tissue that commonly produces fever, altered consciousness, and focal neurological abnormalities; it need not be related to travel.

Acute bacterial meningoencephalitis.description: A life-threatening bacterial infection of the meninges with associated brain dysfunction. Advanced age and neutrophilic CSF warrant consideration despite the relatively preserved CSF chemistry.

case: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved over the past 3 years on weekly adalimumab. He presented with 3 weeks of upper respiratory symptoms (sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, chills) followed 2 weeks later by cramping left calf pain that worsened over 2 days, with swelling extending from the calf to the foot and a purpuric/erythematous rash on the dorsum of both feet. He also reported multiple prior self-limited episodes of similar upper respiratory symptoms. On examination, he was uncomfortable from leg pain and had left ankle synovitis; peripheral pulses were normal.

IgA vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis that often follows an upper respiratory infection and causes lower-extremity purpura and joint inflammation. Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence and assessment for renal involvement can help establish the diagnosis.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, p.normalized_text: Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, potentially associated with adalimumab or Crohn’s disease
Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, p.description: Inflammation of small cutaneous blood vessels producing dependent purpura, sometimes accompanied by arthralgia and edema. Potential triggers include infections, inflammatory bowel disease, and medications such as TNF inhibitors.

Left lower-extremity deep vein thrombosi.description: A clot in a deep leg vein that causes unilateral pain and swelling. Crohn’s disease increases venous thromboembolism risk, and this presentation warrants prompt exclusion with venous ultrasonography even if another condition explains the rash.

Postinfectious reactive arthritis.description: Sterile inflammatory arthritis developing after an infection, usually gastrointestinal or genitourinary but occasionally respiratory. It commonly affects lower-extremity joints asymmetrically.

Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa.description: A skin-predominant vasculitis affecting small and medium muscular arteries, sometimes associated with inflammatory bowel disease or preceding infection. It can cause painful leg lesions, myalgia, and joint symptoms.

case: A 47-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with a six-month history of left-sided sore throat, ipsilateral otalgia, and a six-week history of a left-sided neck mass. He had never smoked and drank less than 5 units of alcohol per week. On examination in the ENT clinic, a firm fixed lymph node was palpable in the upper anterior triangle.

Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, p.normalized_text: Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, potentially HPV-associated
Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, p.description: Cancer of the tonsil or base of the tongue that can present with referred ear pain and cervical lymph-node metastasis. HPV-associated disease can occur in nonsmokers with minimal alcohol exposure. This is the leading concern and requires urgent ENT investigation and tissue diagnosis.

Hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.description: Cancer of the lower pharynx that may cause persistent throat pain, referred ear pain, and metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma.description: Cancer arising behind the nasal cavity, often associated with Epstein-Barr virus. It can present with upper cervical lymphadenopathy and unilateral ear symptoms caused by Eustachian tube obstruction.

Lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes.normalized_text: Lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes or tonsillar tissue
Lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that can enlarge cervical lymph nodes or tonsillar tissue, sometimes producing throat discomfort.

Chronic tonsillitis with reactive cervic.normalized_text: Chronic tonsillitis with reactive cervical lymphadenopathy
Chronic tonsillitis with reactive cervic.description: Persistent tonsillar inflammation can cause throat pain, referred ear pain, and reactive enlargement of nearby cervical lymph nodes.

case: 72-year-old white woman with 10-year history of recurrent cystitis. No systemic symptoms. Physical exam showed slight anemia. Urine cultures were positive for Escherichia coli. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy detected by CT and ultrasound. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and subsequent biopsies were negative for both pathologic lymphoid infiltrate and Helicobacter pylori. Otolaryngologic examination and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Serology for hepatitis C virus and hepatitis B virus was negative. No monoclonal component found in serum protein electrophoresis.

Primary urinary bladder extranodal margi.normalized_text: Primary urinary bladder extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)
Primary urinary bladder extranodal margi.description: A rare, usually indolent bladder lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation, including recurrent cystitis. Negative systemic staging can support a localized bladder origin, but diagnosis requires bladder biopsy.

Recurrent bacterial cystitis.description: Repeated bacterial infections of the urinary bladder, most commonly caused by Escherichia coli. The reported cultures support infection, although infection alone would not exclude an underlying bladder disorder.

Follicular cystitis.description: A benign chronic inflammatory bladder disorder characterized by reactive lymphoid follicles, often associated with recurrent urinary infections. Bladder histology is needed to distinguish it from lymphoma.

Urinary bladder malakoplakia.description: An uncommon inflammatory disorder associated with impaired macrophage bacterial processing, frequently involving the bladder and linked to Escherichia coli infections. Diagnosis requires characteristic findings on tissue biopsy.

Urothelial carcinoma of the urinary blad.normalized_text: Urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder
Urothelial carcinoma of the urinary blad.description: A malignancy of the bladder lining that can cause irritative urinary symptoms resembling cystitis or coexist with urinary infection. It is a less directly supported alternative here because no hematuria, bladder lesion, or bladder biopsy findings are provided.

case: 95-year-old woman admitted after a fall. Medical history includes Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin). Laboratory findings showed elevated white cell count and C reactive protein levels. Urine culture revealed Klebsiella pneumoniae infection. Blood cultures were negative.

Klebsiella pneumoniae urinary tract infe.description: A bacterial urinary tract infection is a leading possibility given the positive urine culture and inflammatory markers. However, urinary symptoms or other clinical evidence are needed to distinguish infection from asymptomatic bacteriuria.

Acute pyelonephritis.description: Infection of the kidney, potentially caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. Older adults may have atypical presentations, but the available findings do not establish upper urinary tract involvement.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria.description: Bacteria in the urine without symptoms attributable to urinary infection, common in older women and people with diabetes. This remains possible because no localizing urinary symptoms are reported; the inflammatory findings would require another explanation.

case: 22-year-old athletic male presented with swelling and locking of the left knee. He had no recent trauma but had several football injuries as a child. Two years prior, he had experienced disabling knee pain.

Osteochondritis dissecans.description: A localized injury to bone beneath joint cartilage that can cause an osteochondral fragment to loosen or detach, particularly in young athletes.

Chronic meniscal tear.description: A tear in the knee's fibrocartilage, sometimes related to an old sports injury; a displaced fragment can obstruct joint movement.

Synovial chondromatosis.description: A benign joint disorder in which the synovial lining produces cartilage nodules that can become loose bodies and cause mechanical symptoms.

Post-traumatic intra-articular osteochon.description: A fragment of cartilage or bone remaining within the joint after an earlier injury, causing intermittent obstruction and irritation.

Tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the kne.normalized_text: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the knee
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the kne.description: A usually benign proliferation of synovial tissue, historically called pigmented villonodular synovitis in its diffuse form, that can cause recurrent pain and swelling.

case: 48-year-old male presented with 1-week history of jaundice, dark brown urine, pale stools, and nausea. Medical history and physical exam were unremarkable. Laboratory findings showed hepatic panel in cholestatic pattern: total bilirubin 117 μmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 66.8 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 173 IU/L, γ-Glutamyltransferase 380 IU/L, Alanine transaminase 468 IU/L. CA19-9 was 11783 IU/mL. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and β2-microglobulin were normal.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Choledocholithiasis.description: A stone in the common bile duct can obstruct bile flow, producing jaundice and occasionally very high CA19-9 levels without cancer.

Extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignancy of the extrahepatic bile ducts that can cause painless biliary obstruction. Markedly elevated CA19-9 raises suspicion but is not diagnostic, particularly during obstruction.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.normalized_text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.description: A pancreatic head tumor can compress the distal common bile duct and cause obstructive jaundice. CA19-9 may be elevated from the tumor, accompanying obstruction, or both.

Ampullary adenocarcinoma.description: A malignancy at the ampulla of Vater that can obstruct bile drainage early in its course, sometimes before other examination findings develop.

Acute viral hepatitis with cholestatic f.normalized_text: Acute viral hepatitis with cholestatic features
Acute viral hepatitis with cholestatic f.description: Acute viral liver inflammation can impair bile excretion and cause jaundice with a cholestatic component. Viral testing and biliary imaging are needed to distinguish it from mechanical obstruction.

case: 80-year-old woman with 6-month history of slowly increasing asymptomatic lumbar subcutaneous mass. History of chronic renal failure requiring dialysis three times weekly for 10 years. Poor compliance with phosphate-binding medications and dietary restrictions. Physical exam showed firm, immobile subcutaneous nodule measuring 9 cm in major axis. Laboratory findings: serum calcium 1.95 mmol/L (normal: 2.05-2.55), serum phosphorus 3.3 mmol/L (normal: 0.74-1.52), serum intact parathyroid hormone 142 ng/L (normal: 10-65), serum creatinine 787 μmol/L (normal: 53-106).

Uremic tumoral calcinosis.description: The most likely diagnosis: large calcium-phosphate deposits in soft tissues caused by disordered mineral metabolism in advanced kidney disease, often associated with hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Metastatic calcinosis cutis associated w.normalized_text: Metastatic calcinosis cutis associated with chronic kidney disease
Metastatic calcinosis cutis associated w.description: Deposition of calcium salts in skin and subcutaneous tissue due to systemic calcium-phosphate imbalance; this overlaps with uremic tumoral calcinosis when deposits form large masses.

Calciphylaxis.description: Calcification and thrombosis of small dermal and subcutaneous vessels, usually in patients with advanced kidney disease, causing ischemic skin injury.

Soft-tissue sarcoma.description: A malignant tumor of mesenchymal tissues that can present as a progressively enlarging, painless, firm mass; imaging and sometimes biopsy are needed to distinguish it from benign or calcific lesions.

Tophaceous gout.description: Deposition of monosodium urate crystals in soft tissues, producing firm, often painless nodules; impaired renal urate excretion can increase risk.

case: 47-year-old female presented to emergency department after being hit while skiing by another skier at high speed from behind. Immediate pain and marked general swelling of the knee joint occurred after impact. Unable to bear weight. Physical exam showed neurovascularly intact limb with no broken skin. No relevant medical, family, or social history.

Tibial plateau fracture.description: A fracture of the upper tibial joint surface that can follow high-energy skiing trauma and cause bleeding into the knee joint.

Anterior cruciate ligament rupture.description: A tear of a major knee-stabilizing ligament, often caused by twisting, hyperextension, or collision during skiing. Rapid swelling may reflect bleeding into the joint.

Multiligament knee injury with possible.normalized_text: Multiligament knee injury with possible spontaneously reduced knee dislocation
Multiligament knee injury with possible.description: High-energy disruption of multiple knee ligaments may dislocate the joint, which can return to alignment before examination. Urgent assessment is needed because vascular injury can occur despite an initially normal neurovascular examination.

Posterior cruciate ligament rupture.description: A tear of the ligament that limits backward movement of the tibia, usually caused by force against the front of a bent knee or severe hyperflexion.

Traumatic patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the kneecap, usually laterally, that may spontaneously reduce and leave acute pain, joint bleeding, and possible cartilage injury.

Traumatic meniscal tear.description: A tear of the knee's fibrocartilage cushioning, often resulting from twisting during sports and sometimes occurring with ligament injuries.

case: A 52-year-old woman presented with complaints of anal pain, constipation, and tenesmus for 3 months before being referred to the hospital. There were no relevant prior illnesses. Rectal digital examination revealed a 6-cm smooth elastic mass on the rectal posterior left side 2 cm from the anal verge. Colonoscopy showed a rectal submucosal bulging. Computed tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the presence of a single 6-cm well-delimited mass, compressing and infiltrating the wall of the medium to low rectum.

Rectal schwannoma.description: A rare nerve-sheath tumor of the rectal wall, usually benign, that can present as a well-circumscribed submucosal mass. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry are required for confirmation.

Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumor.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising in the gastrointestinal wall, with variable malignant potential. Rectal tumors may grow outward and produce a large mass with relatively preserved mucosa.

Rectal leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor that can form a smooth submucosal rectal mass and cause obstructive symptoms when large.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A rare malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum that may present as a bulky intramural or submucosal mass with local invasion.

Tailgut cyst.description: A congenital retrorectal developmental cyst, most often recognized in adult women, that can compress the rectum and occasionally develop infection or malignant transformation.

case: Two-year-four-month-old female with IUGR at birth after C-section at 39 weeks (birth weight 1850 g, length 44.5 cm, head circumference 31 cm; Apgar 9). At 3 months, suspected hearing loss was evaluated by ABR, showing bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss, and hearing aids were placed at 4 months. She had persistent growth delay with weight and height below the 3rd percentile, but normal psychomotor development (sitting at 8 months, walking at 14 months, talking at 13 months). CNS MRI was normal. Genetic testing identified a de novo heterozygous PIK3R1 variant c.1956dupT (p.Lys653*) in exon 15.

PIK3R1-related SHORT syndrome.description: An autosomal dominant disorder affecting growth and insulin signaling, with variable short stature, partial lipodystrophy, characteristic facial features, ocular abnormalities, and delayed dentition. The de novo PIK3R1 truncating variant makes this the leading diagnosis, although formal variant classification and clinical correlation remain important.

IGF1 deficiency.description: A rare genetic disorder of insulin-like growth factor 1 production or function that can cause severe prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, microcephaly, and sensorineural deafness.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: An infection acquired before birth that can cause fetal growth restriction and congenital or early-onset sensorineural hearing loss, sometimes without abnormal brain imaging or early developmental impairment.

Silver-Russell syndrome.description: A growth disorder, usually involving genomic imprinting abnormalities, characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, often with relative macrocephaly, feeding difficulties, and body asymmetry.

3-M syndrome.description: An autosomal recessive skeletal growth disorder associated with severe prenatal and postnatal growth restriction and usually normal intelligence.
